reviews.review_text: I have read thru several letters-that ya'll have written and here is what I think about the Arabs. Yes, I am almost positive they were staring at Jodie from across the way- because I remember what one of them was wearing. 2nd-I think they were trying to take attention "off of" the Arabs- so the audience wouldn't think that it was them being Arab that caused the little girl to disappear- you know- naturally THEY did it type stuff.As for the wimpy stewardess, I agree. The other one was much more butch and could have probably beat up Jodie. But as for the plan with the kid-I am sure the Marshal and the stewardess got together because- the stewardess could make sure the little girls name was not on the list of passengers, and she could be a back up for the Marshal-since stewardess know planes a lot better than Marshals.And something that really plagued me- and the other people I went with said I was nuts- WHY didn't the Marshal show I.D. ? Even if it was fake? Hell, anyone could have had a gun and said they were a marshal. It is upsetting to me, because I have watched lots of movies, even the ones with Tommy Lee Jones and their badge is exposed around their neck, or under their lapel, and they have I.D. I thought that was a poor slip in the movie. It would have made the villain look more credible and you would never have suspected him till later on.Jodie Foster was excellent in the movie- I was like- " go girl"- when she was pulling wires out and making the masks drop down and stuff- I guess she was pretty mad by that point. I also think however that if she DID know the engineering of the plane- she could have forced the pilot to land somewhere by messing around with the wiring,etc..I also thought it have been much better if they had re-written it somehow that Jodie would had almost walked up to the casket and then the audience didn't see WHO was in it.But that would have left out her husband. And/or the villain could have hidden the girl in the casket on the plane and put an air hole in it, and that would have been the LAST place to check.It was a good movie though. It put faith back in me- seeing as I was disappointed that Jodie didn't do Hannibal- but that was excellent with Julianne Moore.

This was one of the most over-hyped movies I've ever seen. I was anticipating a decent thriller and got a B movie made with good equipment. If you are going to make a plausible thriller, you need to make sure it doesn't have as many holes as swiss cheese.There is a fine line between setting up a story and spending too much time on fluff. Flightplan passed this line way before the plane even left the ground. Jodie Foster was decent, but the other supporting actors were pretty bad. Combine this along with some bad writing and unfocused ideas and you have a pretty terrible crash.This movie was not only a waste of money, but time as well and I wouldn't even recommend it to friends as a rental!!

I am not a spoiler. I liked this film and Red Eye earlier this year.Both are women in peril flicks. Which do I like better? It is kind of funny, we had two incoming comet movies one year, two volcano movies, two , you get the idea. Which do I like better? I liked the both.I noticed in a very quick shot of the cockpit that the instrument panel depicts a two engine aircraft. And as you see this is a four engine baby. Watch closely, it is only there for a few seconds.The aircraft appears to be an Airbus A380, due to go into service in two years. Note the straight stairway suitable for two or more abreast. This actually may have been shot in an official AirBus mock-up at Toulouse France.What bugged me was the sound of Ms. Fosters shoes as she walked up and down the aisle. Have you ever head heels clicking on a hard floor in an airplane at 600 mph and 36,000 feet.

I saw this film only last night and I was impressed to find that it was produced by the biggest name in entertainment I know, Brian Grazer. Producer of such films as Splash, The Grinch, Liar Liar and Apollo 13. The film interested me at first with the disappearance of the woman's daughter and wondering whether or not she was crazy or not, that was getting me on the edge of my seat. But I slowly slid back in my seat when it was revealed that her daughter was on the plane and the flight Marshall was planning to blow up the plane. The film should have ended with the woman being crazy and having her convicted to a mental hospital where the spirit of her daughter still haunts her today. The film transformed from psychological thriller to action packed film and I was not too fond of that. I do admit though that the talents of Jodie Foster are truly a classic. So it wasn't bad but it was okay.

reviews.review_text: No spoilers here. I'd give this a 6.5 even though Jodie is a 9 or 10 as usual. The film IS an above average mystery/thriller that DOES capture your attention and holds it grippingly through at least 70% of the film. But, even though the audience's reaction was one of applause (a very rare reaction), the movie's script tends to spiral out of control into some rather obvious amateurish flaws that are a bit difficult to digest and get past. That said, it is a decently fun, entertaining film...especially for Jodie's fans (her acting is, as usual, NOT disappointing)....and there are some clever twists/mysteries in the movie that deserve far more respect than what I've seen other reviewers give it. But, unfortunately, I left the theater wondering why Jodie, presumably, passed up many other offers in the last 3 years to choose this particular film. The producers are VERY, VERY fortunate, indeed, to have her. What this film needed was Alfred Hitchcock's or Brian DePalma's directorial and script-tweaking expertise. JUGGERNAUT

reviews.review_text: Tepid, preposterous thriller about a mother whose child goes missing aboard an intercontinental flight. A potentially intriguing "Lady Vanishes" type premise mangled by outrageous storyline that steers it from psychological thriller to mundane action flick. Visually flashy but utterly lacking in tension or suspense. The always-enjoyable Jodie Foster, plays a mother, trapped in a Kafka-esquire situation, her sanity questioned as she tries to convince a skeptical captain and crew that her child has somehow been snatched aboard the plane. Sadly, Foster is given little to do except look angst-ridden throughout her character's ordeal; Peter Sarsgaard is horribly miscast as an air marshal though Sean Bean is effective as the captain of the high tech airliner. A terrible waste of talent.

Jodie Foster once again gives an outstanding performance in this movie with many twist and turns. An engineer returns to New York along with her daughter and the body of her husband aboard a large airliner. During the flight home her young daughter disappears in mid air. This is the story of the search for her daughter and the many places aboard this giant airliner the we do not usually see. Jodie is really into this role which keeps you at the edge of your movie seat. This is one of the best flicks I have seen in some time, and shows that some Hollywood writers still can write good movie. My suggestion is that you rush right out and see this adventurous movie.

reviews.review_text: FLIGHTPLAN (2005) **1/2 Jodie Foster, Peter Sarsgaard, Sean Bean, Kate Beahan, Marlene Lawston, Erika Christensen. "Panic Room" by way of the "Twilight Zone's "Nightmare at 20,000 Feet" could've been the pitch for this high-concept thriller about a recently widowed aero designer (a never better fiercely feisty Foster) traveling aboard the plane she designed from Germany to New York with her little girl who winds up missing (or disappearing) mid-flight which calls to question the woman's sanity (is she crazy or did she even have a daughter) that will have you guessing amidst the plot holes and a lot to swallow from the screenplay by Peter A. reviews.review_text: The premise is not bad, but unfortunately the movie does not deliver. Jodie Foster, good actress though she might be, seems to have insisted on hogging all footage: there are only 3 scenes in the entire movie in which she does not appear. After an hour of this, it becomes very tedious, and you wish there was a diversion, a comic relief, of a sub-plot. The latter is the most sorely missed: a movie without any sub-plots makes for a single-minded experience. This may have been done to increase the intensity of the movie, but it creates the wrong kind of intensity: one that's tiresome instead of intriguing. I kept looking at my watch hoping for this to end. Also, while this movie is designed to have the audience sympathize with Foster's character, the only emotion it evoked in me was annoyance with her. She is too obsessive and selfish, frightening the other passengers and committing acts of sabotage while in flight in her attempts to find her daughter. I found myself wishing the crew would sedate her.The following is NOT a spoiler but you may still want to avoid reading this until after you've watched the movie: once the mystery is revealed, it is extremely unsatisfying because it is too far fetched and the purpose for which the girl disappears could have been achieved in many other, less convoluted ways. The ending is melodramatic in the extreme, and makes Foster's character even less sympathetic.On the plus side: Good acting by Sean Bean and Peter Sarsgaard

Rarely have I been so annoyed by a film. Perhaps this is because "Flightplan" starts off with such promise before descending (ha ha) into a laughably ridiculous, clichéd, and downright boring final third. The movie develops as a fascinating and emotionally gripping story of a delusional woman who is convinced her dead daughter accompanied her on board as has been kidnapped.**SPOILERS** ... but surprise! She is, in fact, correct! Coincidentally, none of the 500 passengers saw the girl or witnessed her kidnapping. Coincidentally, the air marshal and a flight attendant are in cahoots to orchestrate a hijacking threat, demand a $50 million ransom, and attempt to pin the entire thing (including the on-board ransom demand) on a woman who has no idea what is going on. Right.What surprises me is how far off base Roger Ebert's review was of this film. He writes, "Often in thrillers we think of obvious questions that the characters should be asking, but do not, because then the problems would be solved and the movie would be over." That's right, and "Flightplan" is a textbook example. Jodie Foster's character figures out the entire conspiracy, gains control of the situation, is able to take the hijacker's gun ... and then gives the gun to the captain, has him leave the plane, and seals all the exits so as to be alone with her (surprise!) still-armed foe. Sure, this allows for yet another limping-attacker-slowly-chasing-resourceful-woman climax, but the repeated blatant assaults on the audience's common sense and credulity are simply too much to take."Flightplan" seemed promising as it slowly established the impossibility of the actual explanation it provides. There is the possibility of a good movie in there, but as it stands, "Flightplan" is an enormous cheat.

reviews.review_text: First of all, I loved the movie. But my companion and I are disagreeing over one plot point near the end. When Kyle tells Carson not to leave the plane, why does he listen to her and come back? I say it's because he realized she knew what the plot was and she was deliberately playing her part as the hijacker, daring him to continue the deception by obeying her order. The ideologue supports this, because they both talk about "playing the game" at that point. My friend says that's ridiculous, Carson should have just run away, blown up the plane and still blamed it all on Kyle. I think THAT doesn't make sense because people would have heard her command to him and wondered why he wasn't afraid of her. And, of course, the movie would have been 15 minutes shorter and not have had a happy ending. Does anyone else have an opinion on this? Is my friend right? Does Carson's behavior make no sense at all, other than advancing the plot in the direction it needs to go for the happy ending?As to the captain and the morgue director being the same person, my companion thought so as well, but if that were so, why would Carson and the captain have to have the conversation about wiring the money? The captain would be in on the plot.

reviews.review_text: Jodie Foster is great to watch, but even she will get on your nerves the bozillianth time she screams at a stranger. Where's my daughter?! Somebody took my daughter! Find my daughter! Yes, of course, that is what anyone in the same situation would say, but it does get old fast. So, too, do all the many conveniences that the audience is expected to just accept, and the radically unrealistic turns that happen here and there. The movie does a good job setting up a decent red herring, though once you realize "they" are not the bad guys, you roll your eyes. The opening fifteen minutes are very slow and could have been done in 2 minutes. Once Flightplan gets going, it does keep your interest, though a lot of the searching (for the little girl) feels like the same five minutes over and over again. The 2nd half of the second act is the best of the movie, once Jodie goes awol and realizes for whatever reason (people think she's crazy, there is a conspiracy, etc.) she is on her own. She does the stuff the smart, determined mother always does in these movies, but because she is Jodie Foster it's more believable than, say, Charlize Theron in Trapped or Julianne Moore in The Forgotten. The end of Flightplan and the reveal of the aforementioned conspiracy is pretty lame, and wholly unbelievable, but you do get that moment where Foster wins the day and everybody in the theater applauds. The overall pacing of the movie is hit and miss as it moves along, but I had enough fun while I was watching it that I didn't mind. Like I said, the reveal, or twist, or whatever it was... well, that was silly. I really think they could have come up with something better, but it doesn't ruin the movie. Just makes you roll your eyes, grin, and bear it through yet another bloody-crazy-guy-with-a-gun-is-after-you chase scene. Thankfully Flightplan is not too long, and if you can suspend your disbelief just long enough, you'll have fun. See it if you like shallow action thrillers or Jodie Foster kicking butt with bloodshot eyes.

reviews.review_text: Serious spoilers, don't read if you haven't seen the movie.Overall, the setup was a good time, and for the first half of the film I was entertained and vaguely hoping Jodie Foster would wind up frothing at the mouth in a straitjacket before the end. But it didn't, and instead the director tried to make the ending plausible. Plausibility is impossible because the following questions came to mind during the movie and ruined the whole experience. I have about 100,000 flight miles this year, so pardon me if I sound a little jaded. -How did they know she would fall asleep? -How did she get past the gate without running the girls boarding pass through the machine? -How did they know which flight she would take home, and how could they guarantee the flight attendant would be on board? -How could the air marshal get that seat? His flight attendant girlfriend has no control of the seating. -Why would she be boarded early unless she was a 'special needs' passenger (i.e. with children)? -Just how did the air marshal know this plane so well, and how could he get past the galley without disturbing one passenger or crew member? -Why did they only call the morgue? Why not the police? -Why didn't they shoot her in the head when she stood at the door?I really wanted to suspend disbelief, but all of the bull drove me crazy. Cap it off with everyone saying "That's her daughter!" and the politically correct ending, and you walk away feeling like you ate an ice cream cone that only had one scoop on the top and nothing but an empty waffle at the bottom. 5/10

Right from the start, this film had me guessing. Is Kyle Pratt (an American aircraft propulsion engineer living in Germany) imagining that eerily deserted subway station? Or, is she imagining the coffin at the mortuary? Then, once it's been established that she did, indeed, recently become a widowed mother, I got to see her bond with Julia, her six year-old daughter. This instantly builds up the sympathy factor for both of them.When Kyle wakes up from a nap, atop some empty mid-aisle seats, the tension really begins. I knew what she was going to find--or rather not find--from movie trailers. But, still, my nervousness increased with hers, as she searched every level of this newfangled luxury airliner...and no Julia.And, the initially co-operative crew members quickly become all too skeptical as to Julia's existence. Especially after the pilot (masterfully played by Sean Bean of "National Treasure" fame) receives a communique' that MR. Pratt didn't die alone! It's ultimately revealed, of course, that Kyle isn't suffering from grief-stricken delusions or hallucinations. I will not, however, reveal the motivations behind the psych-warfare campaign that's been conducted against her. Suffice it to say that the Chief Bad Guy is someone I didn't suspect, at all. And, that he makes Cillian Murphy's character, from "Redeye," look like a Boy Scout, by comparison. *Which is saying a lot, because I saw the latter film twice!*In short, Jodie Foster outdoes the nail-biting performance she gave in "Panic Room." And, I heartily recommend this flick to anyone else who doesn't mind sitting--quite literally--on the edges of their seats. In fact, it's such a good movie, you won't even mind the fact that the question of why those Arab-American tourists lied (about being across the street from the Pratt family's German townhouse) is never answered!

reviews.review_text: This is an example of the bane of any director who chooses to make a smart thriller - how do u end it?! Let's get the bad out of the way first - Sarsgaard for some inexplicable reason walks sleepy-eyed thru' most of the movie... but that's pardonable... The greatest falling of this movie would be the tripe, convenient ending - it almost appears as if the director was in a sudden hurry to wrap the movie off, and all the chips very conveniently fell in place... This creates a few loopholes and "Huh??? How did that happen?" kinda moments...But as far as I am concerned, that is it... Everything else above the movie is first rate... Lemme start with the performances - WHY ISN'T JODIE FOSTER DOING MORE MOVIES??!!! She is stunning in the movie as a troubled, confused and incredibly determined mother and bereaving wife - her performance is utterly convincing and u feel for her... Another great performance is by Sean Bean (Boromir of the LOTR fame) - his sensitive portrayal of the flight captain is laudable! Very controlled, very classy...But above all, this is the director's movie - the failings are his, and the achievements are his alone - the first 75% of the movie is simply spectacular... gripping... as good as any Hitchcock movie ever made. The suspense is absorbing, the plot is a thriller. The director brings us to the edge of our seats and manages to keep us there, completely absorbed in the web he weaves, for nearly 2/3rds of the film... There is really nothing that can be nit-picked upon in this part of the movie - it is frankly, faultless! Attaboy! And the problems I have with the ending, are probably accentuated by the fact that such a stunning beginning deserved an exceptional climax, and it didn't get one...All in all, a definite big-screen must-see... It would be criminal to deny Ms. Foster and her director the audience they rightly deserve!

reviews.review_text: "Flightplan" is a well made and watchable film. It could have been much better but the filmmakers seem like they could not decide what they wanted to do with the film.If they wanted this to be a top-notch thriller, they would have had to come up with a better twist to the story or have a more convincing villain. If they had wanted this to be a frivolous action film, then they would have put some humor in the film. Instead, they did neither and the ending is so ridiculous that it is not very satisfying."Flightplan" has the same basic premise as "The Forgotten" but does not have the self effacing humor and despite having an absurd twist, it takes itself way too seriously.The film is saved by immaculate technical detail. The directing, photography, and acting are all first rate. The music if atmospheric without being intrusive."Flightplan" is decent entertainment but it could have been much better if they had fixed the screenplay.

This awe-consuming thriller is intriguing and interesting right to the last minute, without crossing the boundary of boredom  a fantastic achievement for a film with such a concentrated focus for a story line. The acting was top class and completely realistic - it really makes an impact on you both whilst watching the film and in the following weeks. Although its a hard scenario to believe is possible, you couldn't fault the film as it ironed out any flaws in arguments as to why it's impossible. The suspense in the film was reflected throughout the audiences reaction in the cinema and with a clever and surprising twist at the end; you definitely don't want to miss it

reviews.review_text: Just another typical plot twist storyline. I wasn't surprised.Want to know just how many times in the real world an airline employee and a federal agent (especially law enforcement) have ever been involved with a hijacking. The answer-- NoneIn the real world, over 99% of hijackers have been carried out by one group. In fact, you could say this group "invented" hijacking. But of course, the nice man at the end was sure to hand back the dropped teddy bear. Spare me the attempt to make me feel guilty over ever suspecting that a member of a particular group could have been the real hijacker.

The only redeeming feature of Flightplan is that kept you mildly entertained to the end, which was gratefully not too drawn out i.e. it wasn't a 2hr+ academy-wannabe-crapfest, but only a 1.5hr crapfest, thankfully.This movie must have one of the most ridiculously contrived plots of all time I must say! And it seems to be just another vehicle for Foster's feminist lesbian "I never wanna kiss or be with a man on screen again" BS. At least in this one she has a husband, even if he's dead at the start LOL, unlike Panic Room where there was an immaculate conception & no man anywhere to be seen! I don't dislike Foster, but she's really strayed from the movies that made her great & she doesn't seem to make any effort to connect with her audience any more, but only seems to make movies that have some "message" or "artistic" worth only she can see. This one really borders on the ridiculous as far as suspension of disbelief goes and as another poster said, it just throws way too much misleading irrelevancy into the fray which only detracts & distracts from a plot which really can't afford it.Gone are your great days of Silence, Nell, The Accused & Contact Ms Foster.

This seems a good movie for watching, but just for once. You can follow the story and enjoy it. But this is not as well as another one made so long time ago.What I would mention here is that there is a similar movie in 1965. The name is "Bunny Lake Is Missing", directed by Otto Preminger, starting Laurence Olivier, Carol Lynley and Keir Dullea. I saw the movie long time ago, but I found the same plot summary for both of them. What idea that makes both of them interesting is that the viewer does not know the truth since a while. The ambiguity that is made for the first role, also is made for watcher. But I think, "Bunny Lake Is Missing" a better movie.In the first one, the reason of story is money, but in "Bunny Lake Is Missing", psychological interests make the reason. In comparison between them, I believe that "Bunny Lake Is Missing" is stronger than the "Flightplan", both from story line point of view and acting. Consider just about 40 years have been passed.

reviews.review_text: I've seen plenty of dumb movies with ludicrous premises and unbelievable plots ("Armageddon" in particular), but seldomly saw a movie that start off okay only to go off the deep end to the depth of the bottomless pit of stupefying idiocy.Flightplan is the fine example of typical degenerate Hollywood idiocy that treat the audiences like naive children. That the fact this film and its crew go out of the way to insult the intelligence of the audience is beyond rationale.Flightplan is a dumb and depraved film that believe it can pull the tricky plot effect a la The Sixth Sense and still expect the audience to swallow such absurdities. It's like the script was written with Crayola on index notes to scatter in a recycle bin and salvage randomly to pick paper thin plot points and airtight thin character development to hand over to the group of highly intelligent chimpanzees to bang out the D-grade direct-to-video TV script on Final Draft computer.It astounds me that Jodie Foster, Peter Sarsgaard and (he was awesome as a bad guy in Patriot Games) Sean Bean waste their talent on this POS. Didn't they know how implausibly ridiculous Flightplan script is? They must have green dollar signs ka-ching in their eyeballs and proceed to sink to act in a movie that would have headed to 1.99 direct-to-video bin trash if not for producer Brian Grazer who has the knack for sentimental cheesepuff and dumb-sh*t movies.Flightplan is basically the hybrid of the somewhat tense but disappointingly weak Panic Room and that predictable 1996 Mel Gibson movie Ransom. That the film incorporate such blatant racism against a specific Middle Eastern race is pretty insensitive and insulting.Hollywood producers seem to believe anything profound can be slapped onto the hackneyed script. They're in it to con the audiences into coughing up hard-earned money to see such movies that mock, pander and condescend rather than entertain with at least a fairly plausible story.Flightplan is pure fantasy that blatantly disregard common sense and logic. This is profoundly disdainful that ask the audiences to stretch the limit in suspension of disbelief beyond acceptable level. Armageddon was intended as an action fantasy movie and it accomplishes that purpose. Flightplan, however, pretend to be a serious thriller-drama movie that proceed to sink itself into morbid Hollywood fantasyland towards the end.That the hideous quality of this film show the crew -- including the hack committee-paid screenwriters, greedy credit-coveting producers and coke-dealer-for-hire director -- care far more about showing the pretentiously splendid visuals than send the draft back in for further revision to eliminate the ridiculous plot elements and up the dose of plausibility or it goes out to be thrown into the pile of bad scripts in the blue recycle bin.One of the worst films I've ever seen for such ludicrously unbelievable plot concepts that demand I leave my brain at the door. Chalk this up with "serious yet riddled with moronic logic" movies such as Armageddon and Twister.Zero stars

reviews.review_text:
OK, imagine you paid, like, $10 to sit for two hours in this awesome show. And at first you really like what's going on on stage -- good visuals, thrill, suspense and whatnot.

And then, all of a sudden, some door at the side of the theater pops open, spilling out -- a horde of loud, vulgar clowns! The clowns start to dance around your seat, point at you, throw food at you and start to chant "You're stoopid!" with this annoying french accent. And they just won't stop!

So, how is this related to "Flightplan"? Way more than you initially might have thought -- because, really, this is what actually expects you if you pay to see this movie: A great start, Jodie Foster doing fine, and then suddenly some "plot" twist (or is it the desperate attempt to mend plot holes by dropping an atom bomb on them?), that insults your intelligence more than any horde of clowns would be able to if they had a year's time.

For that, I hate this movie! And if you have already paid, and actually liked "Flightplan", you might very well deserve to have food thrown at you -- stoopid!

reviews.review_text: If Jody Foster is in something I usually expect it to at least be a decent film...but not even the great Ms. Foster can save this one. After about 15 minutes of her ranting I was ready to issue parachutes to everyone so they could escape because at least I could change the channel...And yes I am so glad I saw this at home...in fact I didn't even have to rent it. If they had added some supernatural element then maybe they could have saved this bad script writing. Alas it is not to be. Instead we are given bad writing upon bad writing which no amount of good acting (which most of the actors did)can save...By the time she finds her daughter my "suspension of disbelief" had long since expired and I found myself not caring about any of the characters. After all, it was just a movie...a bad one...but just a movie none the less.

Jodie Foster must have been either desperate for work, or didn't bother to read the script to this senseless drivel. Her character, Kyle Pratt, is a propulsion engineer (fancy name for jet engine designer) for a new type of plane. She is "chosen" by the hijacker as a target based on her knowledge of the plane. When her daughter disappears during the flight, nobody seems to have noticed that she ever boarded the plane. Nobody on board seems to believe Kyle that she had anyone with her and they suggest that she is making it up. During her search for the child, she finds her way into the avionics and cargo bays and short circuits some of the systems (still not sure how that was meant to help her find the girl). Here are the two main inconsistencies: 1) There is no way that a jet engine specialist would know a plane so intimately that she would be able to identify every hatch and avionic system.2) The entire hijack plan is based on the belief, or at least hope, that none of the 400+ passengers on the plane would notice the little girl boarding (and they don't in this movie...) What are the chances of that happening in real life?A most annoying aspect is that they haven't bothered to build a plausible looking model of this supposedly revolutionary plane - the E474 (give me a break, couldn't they have thought up something more original?) The shots of the "plane" sitting on the tarmac, taking off and landing are about as believable as watching "Thunderbirds", but at least THEY didn't try to pass them off as the real thing. This movie explores a few social issues too. That of herd mentality (the passengers' mood sways every time there is a new development), and of course the mandatory Arab suspect (played by one Mr. Cohen). These cheep shots simply add to the cringe factor.Despite all this, Jodie Foster is excellent as usual, as is Peter Sarsgaard. The acting in general is OK. I don't regret watching the movie, but they should have done more with the script (ie throwing away the original and rewriting it completely).

For any film to be successful, there are many aspects that must come together, not the least of which is a good story. Imagine then, if you will, how the writer might have made his pitch to the producer for this one..."Like, okay...a recent widow (and an aeronautic engineer, too) is flying back to USA with her daughter and her husband's body in a casket. After the plane's been flying for three hours, the woman discovers her daughter is missing and goes almost berserk trying to find her  unaware that she's being manipulated by a pair of killers who have a plan to extort fifty million bucks from the airline company..." Sounds like The Lady Vanishes, from Hitchcock. Forget it."No, look, okay...this is a plane, not a train. It's all up in the air, y'know. Thirty-thousand feet." So am I. What's the plot, anyway? You got two more minutes..."She gets on the plane with her kid. When she wakes up, the kid's gone. Nobody admits to seeing her. And, there's a kicker..." Oh, yeah? Better be good."Yeah, it is: the plane's manifest has no daughter listed! She never was, baby, never. Or...was she? Doncha just love it?"Get to the point, fer Pete's sake!"Well, the bad guys altered the manifest, so that everybody would think the woman's insane  especially when she rushes around the plane, into all the nooks she knows about, being an engineer and all, and starts to make things unpleasant for the captain and passengers."Lemme get this right: you're saying we have a nutcase as a heroine? "No, no  not really. She only looks like it." (Pause) "I was thinking of Jodie Foster in the role, what with all her experience in Lambs, Panic Room, The Accused, y'know?" Go on...but, I'm getting ready to do my impression of Kevin Spacey in Sharks, so watch it."Well, okay, I be quick. She squirms all over the damn plane, looking, searching, y'know, and finally gets to the casket with the stiff, y'know, her dead husband. So, she opens it, she's frantic, she wants to commune with her husband's spirit, sort of..."Wait a minute: so, the kid's in the casket, right?"No, no, no...the bad guys wanted her to open it, that's all." What the hell for? You got thirty seconds..."Ah-ha...that's one of the big secrets!" Spare me. What next?"The captain  I'd suggest Sean Bean for this one, great tough looking guy  puts the flight marshal in charge of her when they find her there, sobbing inta the coffin. Then they head for an emergency landing to get rid of the nutcase...er...the heroine." Bean? Doesn't he always play the bad guy? Ten seconds..."Well, then the real bad guy  who's now revealed to all the audience  tells the captain that the woman is trying to extort the fifty million bucks and gets the airline to agree  while funneling the money to his own account electronically. Then he plans to kill her and the daughter..." Okay, that's enough. This is one of the most ridiculous and convoluted plots you ever threw at me. It's just absurd to think that an extortionist would go to those lengths  the need for a dead body, a woman who knows airplanes, who has the required psychology, not to mention a daughter, and the guts to tell a whole aircrew to shove it while she tries to take a plane apart in mid-air..."But, it's got a great finish, a nail-biter, almost a parody of Terminator when she ices the bad guy." Hmmm, that good? So, who else do you recommend?"Well, I was thinking of Pete Sarsgaard as the Flight Marshal. He did real good in Jarhead and Boys Don't Cry, y'know."Yeah, yeah. So, it's all in and on a plane, right?"Yeah, well, except for a bit of back story..."So, it could all be done on the cheap, right, just a couple of airplane mockups, right?"No problem. Real cheap, for sure. Well, except for the actors and what all..." Yeah, yeah, okay  you'll get yours, don' worry. Look, tell ya what: you work a full treatment for me in, say, a week and I'll bounce it off a few of the execs around, see what comes back."A week? Hey, man, that's pushing it." Okay, well, I dunno who'd ever want to see this one, if that's the way you feel..."Okay, okay, I'll do a rush job, go without food, burn the candles, just for you, okay!" Well, we all gotta fill our quotas, man. Even if it is cheap, know what I mean?

Flightplan raises a lot of questions throughout its runtime, some of which are at first ambiguous but later solved; some of which are frustrating to begin with but when the time comes, you wish you weren't told the answer and some of which are just left unanswered anyway due to the film's veering into the entertainment category nearer the end. The film is like an athlete in a marathon: they've trained and trained but on the final day, they've treated it like a sprint and used up all their energy in the opening stages. That means that by the time the end of the road is in sight, they are quite literally crawling over the line; they finish but it is a struggle by the end.This is Flightplan; a film that opens up like a horror/thriller but by the end has twisted and turned so much, its even confused itself. When the film ends, you feel as if you don't want to go back and try to discover and uncover what's what and what's right because the film has done such a good job in seducing and engaging the audience. It's practically impossible to talk about Flightplan without giving away certain things but Flightplan forces you to pay attention, much like the twists in The Crying Game and The Village, if you pay attention and observe everything on the screen that you're given then you'll crack the case before it's given to you. What did it for me similarly to The Crying Game was in the form of certain attributes within a certain character  look closely at the plausibility and physical attributes of certain people and ask yourself if they could possibly be what they say they are.Flightplan is the sort of film that starts off with the traditional establishing of a prior event that acts as a tragedy for the protagonist and in this case, it's the death of Kyle Pratt's (Foster) husband who she is transporting, in a coffin, from Germany to the United States for burial. The coffin may play more of a role later on than you would think although by that time we have to be force fed the logic and the scares rather than rely on suspense. But this prior tragedy of the dead husband doesn't just act as a plot MacGuffin and nor is it used purely to further the plot later on when required. The dead husband back-story adds a certain urgency to Pratt's panic when she is on the plane and has lost her child  it is this motherly figure who has lost her partner and is now in the position of crisis having failed to protect her young.But despite Flightplan's failings later on when certain characters reveal their plans and a certain narrative begins to unravel, it remains for the best part and interesting and gripping film predominantly revolving around paranoia. Flightplan had me; it had be sucked into its world, into its grasp and then just began to let me go  it is a bizarre almost physical feeling that you get when it descends into its final act and teeters on breaking into a mere action film. The causality the film displays in its opening hour is perfectly legitimate even if it is allowed through some pretty brain dead logic involving how the child had vanished from her seat in the first place. So if the atmosphere of "have I, haven't I seen your child" works; the desperation and interaction between Kyle and Captain Rich (Bean) and the general feeling you get when the daughter does go missing is damn good, how come the film falls flat? It is simple. After an eerie scene in which Kyle has a bash at some Arab characters in a scenario that plays out like: 'agitated woman on a plane accuses some Arabs of wrong doing', the film begins to give away who's who and what's what  the film unravels its secrets and its ideas but we retain the point of view from Kyle and she remains the focus. The difference between focusing on Kyle and not knowing where the girl is and focusing on Kyle but knowing where the girl is and who's who is huge. The film dissipates; it lets out three quarters of its air in one scene when someone confronts someone else and tells them of the plan. From here, the remaining quarter of suspense evaporates in due course. It's as if it doesn't want to be a thriller any more. When Kyle is made to look like the bad guy, the film has become a meandering if not very familiar action film. It has become a chase film in which a slightly physically deformed psycho is chasing a young woman in a location she cannot escape from. Sound familiar? Yes, it's a slasher film premise.So how disappointing for a film to start out so smart; for a film to be produced through America but with a German (European) director; only to end so disappointingly. The film begins with the establishing of a situation, the establishing of another on and the development of a good idea  but it ends with an explosion in typical generic proceedings. The film is no disaster but it refrains from being one of those great twist films you like to revisit every once in a while.

reviews.review_text: When waking up on a plane, Kyle Pratt finds her daughter missing, but no one can recall Pratt ever bringing her daughter aboard.The plot outline sounded fantastic and with the excellent montage to open, I had very high expectations as I sat back and put my feat up ready to be entertained, but by the end, I simply felt confused and let down.Jodie Foster (Silence of the lambs) stars as Kyle Pratt, and gives a good performance as the grief-stricken aviation engineer. And as good as she is, it is due to the script that lets the film down, with little and boring dialogue and an inconsistency that ruins what could have been a tremendous exciting narrative.The plot is very inconsistent through many stops and starts in the event to try and track down the missing daughter. The plot and the pilots try and remain professional but come across as being slightly silly and very far-fetched and unrealistic in its own context.The use of the plane could have added more to the nausea of the genre but was poorly used. Though the wide space and dimension is sued, none of the timing and situation is executed as efficiently and exciting to justify the true meaning of the genre.There is also a feeling of inevitability about who the villain is, but there are a few twists encoded to keep the viewers guessing. However these twists put me out of the plot and into another idea as to what was happening and made the plot muddled.Despite the flaws in the plot, there is still a feeling of excitement as regards to what has actually happened to the child, helped along by some drastic measures. Like many in the claustrophobic thriller genre, there isn't much realism but still an ability to keep you glued to your seat to find out what has happened.There are plenty of unanswered questions left hanging at the quite ridiculous climax, but there are good performances and an exciting feel that will keep you entertained to the end

reviews.review_text: Flightplan starts in Berlin in Germany as grieving widow Kyle Pratt (Jodie Foster) & her young six year old daughter Julia (Marlene Lawston) board a flight to New York, together with her dead husband in the cargo hold who they intend to bury back in the US the plane takes off for it's long journey to New York. Kyle & Julia both fall asleep, when Kyle wakes up Julia has gone. At first Kyle thinks Julia is wandering around somewhere but after checking the plane Kyle can see no sign of her daughter. Becoming increasing worried about her missing daughter Julia demands that the plane is searched, Captain Rich (Sean bean) is unsure what to think as no-one remembers even seeing Julia & she is no present on the passenger manifesto either. With no record of Julia ever having boarded the plane Kyle's accusations are not taken seriously but she know's that Julia is somewhere on the plane & Kyle is going to find her...Directed by Robert Schwentke one has to say that for two thirds of it's duration Flightplan is a neat little mystery thriller in the vein of Alfred Hitchcock's classic The Lady Vanishes (1933) although here instead of an old woman disappearing on a train a young girl goes missing on a plane, unfortunately the final third is a bit of a mess that really stretches credibility. While the first two thirds are nicely done with a gradual build-up of suspense & tension revolving around the mysterious disappearance of a young girl the explanation offered during the final third is just daft & full of plot holes. It seem like after a slow yet interesting first two thirds of Flightplan the makers decided they needed to up the action & pace & turned it into an action thriller with fights, shooting, explosions & the expected face-off between the heroine & villain. Some of the plot holes are gaping & too big to ignore like the idea that an airline would pay a huge ransom to a terrorist they have never even spoken to, how does the villain expect to get the money anyway? What proof doe they have it was ever really deposited in the bank account? The idea that a woman can get on a plane with a young girl & no-one notices the girl is absurd, the kidnapping & hiding of the girl again without anyone seeing anything is hard to believe & the villains plan was over complicated anyway relying on many coincidences, luck & pure chance to succeed as how did they manage to get themselves on the same flight as Kyle? How did they know for certain Kyle would go crazy & actually open the coffin? How were they going to make sure they were there when Kyle did open the coffin? Kidnapping a young girl in a plane cabin full of passengers is risky to say the least, what if Kyle hadn't gone to sleep or if Julia had woken up & screamed? At 90 odd minutes it moves along at a decent pace & while it does get very silly at the end the first two thirds are really quite good. The character's are thin, no-one is given any sort of background & even Kyle is very shallow as a character while her daughter barely gets two lines. There's also a quick stab at reversing expectations as the blatantly suspicious looking Arab guy's prove to be good blokes while the so-called all American hero protector on the flight turns out to be slime.The film is pretty stylish as it goes with nice clean bright cinematography, there's no shaking camera here or quick machine gun editing. The film mixes suspense & tension & all out action with mixed results, the build-up is good & intriguing while the pay-off is loud, noisy & has zero credibility. The CGI computer effects are alright, they can't even film a proper plane taking off now it has to be a CGI computer effect. Not much violence until the last third & only one person dies in the whole thing anyway. It's just a pity that the script couldn't come up with a more plausible explanation for the first two thirds of the Flightplan which are suspenseful, it's like every time one idea is used to cover a plot hole or explain something it raises more questions & plot holes.With a supposed budget of about $55,000,000 this had a lot of money spent on it, personally I think the same years Red Eye (2005) is much better overall as a woman finds herself kidnapped & blackmailed on a plane. The acting is OK, Jodie Foster is alright but doesn't bring much to Kyle, Sean Bean is wasted while Peter Sarsgaard is pretty good.Flightplan is a film that I liked , sure the first two thirds are so much better than then eventual explanations & far fetched Hollywood thriller reasonings but overall I liked it. Not a great film by any means but a good one none the less if you can accept a few lapses in logic at the end.

This is a good performance by Foster and a credible performance by Sarsgaard and Bean. But sadly, their efforts are wasted on a bad executed idea. The idea itself is good, but it's simply difficult to make a 90-minute movie on an airplane. This is a really long 30-minute movie. Despite that, it is still enjoyable to watch Foster play her part extremely well. What could have been done differently? Well, some of the things leading up to the flight should have been included. The flight is the climax of the movie, no doubt - but we don't have much of a chance to identify with the characters because there is so little development. It's like a one-act play where we don't really expect the characters to change much.

1 October 2005. Warning: Spoilers. While Jodie Foster does a decent job of acting the frantic mother, unlike Air Force One (1997), a action thriller, Flight Plan is most strictly a thriller that can only go so far on an airplane. The movie is almost as confining as the script that really couldn't be stretched far enough. We have Jodie character and daughter appearing to get on the plane before anyone else. We have the somewhat unbelievable climatic scorching of an ending that also become even more pedestrian with the survivors' comments. There are so good emotional crowd scenes and some reflection of prejudice and bias in the movie that can't really be developed much. The strain on being an psychological thriller versus an action thriller is again limited and the technological, fancy machination that may have been possible wasn't achieved in this movie. The interpersonal dynamics were visible but just didn't rise to their potential. Five out of Ten Stars.

reviews.review_text: "City of God" director, Fernando Meirelles, does NOT disappoint with his film translation of the John Le Carré novel "The Constant Gardener." His treatment of the violence is on par with "COG." Subtly shown, emotionally felt, yet not glorified. In comparing the slums I've personally seen in South America, I'm drawn to the Kenyan slums on film, because of the way Fernando renders them. Yes, they are terrible, but you really don't want to look away. Unfortunately, I have not read the novel; therefore I cannot draw conclusions (this situation will be remedied next week).Major kudos to Ralph Fiennes for choosing Fernando Meirelles as director and to Richard McCabe, Pete Postlethwaite, Rachel Weisz, Bill Nighy, Hubert Koundé, Gerard McSorley for a job well done  they're a fabulous cast. "The Constant Gardener" is a visually alive, emotionally moving film, not as ferocious as "City of God" but thought-provoking nonetheless.Personally, I found Mr. Meirelles focused, curious, not at all jaded & cynical, down-to-earth, warm and compassionate. He conducted a Q&A after the screening of "The Constant Gardener" in Washington, DC last night. At the post-screening reception, Mr. Meirelles graciously made himself accessible to all attendees. I hope the lovely people of Venice accept "The Constant Gardener" to their festival!! Mr. Meirelles is currently making a new movie that, through the effects of globalization, unites 5 different stories of people, spanning a myriad of cultures in Brazil, China, Kenya, NYC and the desert. Best of Luck!

reviews.review_text: I think the director and the script were a bad match.The dynamic shooting style that he so brilliantly applied to City of God feels inappropriate in service of this rather conventional, overlong, dialogue-driven international thriller.Extreme camera angles and moves are favored over acting and interpersonal drama. These are great actors, but they've been better in other movies. I don't think the director is quite up to the task of directing a mature, "adult" film.And the script is a bit of a mess as well. Too much preachy, naive & on-the-nose dialogue. And the dialogue is doing too much of the dramatic heavy lifting: too much of the crucial action is off-screen or merely referred to in dialogue instead of SHOWN On screen! It felt like a rough draft of what could have been a much better script.Fiennes' character is not very well defined, so when the movie shifts from being her story to his, we're not attached enough to him to care.And there is no real suspense or mystery to his journey: we already pretty much know everything there is to reveal.This leads to an insufferably boring and overlong second half.So much talent here, but mismatches and an underdeveloped script sink it.Don't buy the self-important ads, this one doesn't deliver.

I saw it at a screening recently and was drawn into this great film from the very opening shot. The director does a great job of telling a complex story in an interesting way. His pace and visual technique kept the film moving in a languid yet urgent way (I say this because I remember thinking that there were very few quick cuts in the film, yet I never felt the "drag" that is usually associated with bad pacing). The cast was first rate and the script gave them lots to work with. Mr. Fiennes will likely get an Oscar nod for his performance, it reminded me of his great work in "The English Patient". Rachel Weisz was great too, but I felt she didn't get enough screen time to truly show off her talents.I hope it reaches a wide audience.

reviews.review_text: Over the years I have come to think of Peter Travers as the most clueless movie critic in the media. When I see a rave review by him, I am forewarned. He raved about this movie. I was forewarned. I went anyway. Foolish me. This movie was bad on almost every level. Maybe every level. It was shot in a cinema verite way that was trying to be artistic but only succeeded in being annoying. It was long, boring and had such a fizzle of a payoff that I would have felt cheated if I hadn't given up hope for this mess long before the ending. The message part of the movie was slathered on with a trowel and akin to those World Help ads that you see on Sundays on TV. The movie handled it's delivery so poorly that I was on the side of the evil drug companies and beginning to think that maybe Mugabe has a point. As opposed to the English Patient which had the more discerning in the audience screaming at Feinnes, "Die already", this movie had me wanting to scream, "Kill him already." And I won't spoil it by telling you if they did or not. It's spoiled long, long before you find out one way or another anyway.

Intelligent and moving political thriller that should be held right up there with "All The Presidents Men" and "The Killing Fields " as one of the best political thrillers ever made. Fernando Meirelles tops his last directional effort with a thriller that is moving, scary and down right forthright in it's views of big companies gone wrong and the horrors that they are willing to inflect on others for the sake of profit. Rachel Weisz and Ralph Fiennes give career best performances in this film and that's a huge compliment considering the fact that they are good in almost everything they do, even in bad movies. Weisz is strong willed and obsessive and Fiennes is determine and endearing and both of them compliment each other with there destine to be award winning chemistry and acting chops. The director compliments both of them with a view of Africa that is rarely seen in film and a sense of reality that is only found in real life.Rachel Weisz, Ralph Fiennes and Fernando Meirelles all should be honored at award season for their amazing efforts in this film because as of right now, this is with out a doubt the film to beat come Oscar time.

reviews.review_text: I saw this movie at a Q&A (with the director) screening Sunday night in Lincoln Center. I would say it was good movie but not a great one.It seemed to me that the film was trying to do and be too many things, so the emotional impact it had on me was far less than what I think it should have been, given the basic story and quality of the performances. I never read the book, so I can't compare the film to it.I think my major problems were these: 1.The way the story is told never enabled me to really feel the level of love that was supposed to exist between ""Justin" (Ralph Fiennes) and "Tessa" (Rachel Weisz), and it was this love that was supposed to enable "Justin" to change and choose the course of action that is the center of the story- the protagonist's "quest".2.While the scenes of the conditions the Kenyans and Sudanese (I believe that a later scene was shot in Sudan) live under made me feel sympathy (and to some degree, guilt), there wasn't one main character who was a native of this environment- they were nameless faces who were supposed to symbolize the results of the exploitation and corruption that victimize Africa and her people. (I don't think the doctor who "Tessa" worked with was native to that area.) So, while I felt bad in the same way I would if I were watching the nightly news, it's not the same level of connection I would feel if there had been some well-defined characters- even one- who could have defined "who," as opposed to "what" "Tessa" was fighting for.Because the movie has a mystery element to it, "Tessa's" full motives, by virtue of both the narrative form and needs, retains a degree of mystery, and to me, this made her character seem somewhat aloof, underdeveloped and one-note, although I have no problem with Rachel's portrayal of her. She is quite an engaging actress; reminds me a lot of Kate Winslet .The most successful part of the film to me, despite the roadblocks I mentioned, was Ralph Fienne's beautiful performance. His work here is very internal, subtle and understated, and I found it quietly moving and powerful. Although "the too much going on" I referred to causes a competition of sorts among the elements for what the focus of the film should be- a murder mystery? A love story? An exploration and indictment of government and corporate greed being able to flourish unnoticed in Africa because nobody cares? The director's formidable skill in using flashback, visuals and sound to create auras of haunting memories, mystery, and suspense?- it is Fienne's moving portrayal of an English gentleman who experiences his emotions quietly as he pieces together what has happened that emerges from all of these vying elements as the center of this film.

reviews.review_text: Films that are written as thrillers, suspense stories and romances all feature certain story elements that define the genre. How the elements are combined to tell a specific story is the measure of a story's success at convincing an audience of its worth. "The Constant Gardener" is a well-crafted story with many fine performances, starting with Ralph Fiennes and Rachel Weisz, and including the many character actors who make this film feel viscerally real and true. In the tradition of films like "Silkwood", "Z" and" The Insider", the director of "City of God" takes the audience on a tense, suspenseful ride with characters who dare tell truth to power. The film viewing experience feels dangerous and worth-while. No doubt, "The Constant Gardener", like "City of God" will fuel discussion about the politics which is the basis of this film, and will also send more people to read John Le Carre's book, which is the basis of the film.

reviews.review_text: Not absolutely sure if there is a spoiler herein, but to be safe, please be warned, since this film is, on one level, a mystery drama. One the many wonderful aspects of this film is watching Justin (Fiennes) grow from a detached, kind-hearted, naif to a sad, wise person of the world. And in true LeCarre style, no one is what they seem to be, which adds to the suspense element. The director is also responsible for the remarkable and very hard-hitting "City of God". Now this film comes along and it makes me want to know more about him. He certainly is able to deliver a powerful social message along with a great story. Not many can do that without sounding like they're preaching. I don't want to reveal too much, so I urge you simply to walk into the theater and let this film catch you up in its frenetic, urgent and beautiful style.Ten stars.

reviews.review_text: Great romantic thrill ride that is made even more special by the performances of Rachel Weisz and Ralph Fiennes, who both give this adaptation of the John Le Carre book a real sense of beauty, dignity and grace with their on target performances. Weisz is perfection as Tessa Qualye, a civil rights activist who is murdered for trying to bring awareness of their illegal practices on the poor natives of an African village. Weisz gives her character a self-righteous drive that is made poignant by her determination and sheer will and she also makes her character human, not a stereotype, which makes her performance the more real. Ralph Finnes plays her grieving husband Justin, who takes up her cause and begins to lean of how wonderful his wife really was and what he missed during the time she was alive. His haunted performance is in my opinion his best ever and is the driving point of this haunting odyssey of justice, lost and self sacrifice. Rachel Weisz and Ralph Fiennes both deserve Oscar nominations for their superb performances and Fernando Meirelles deserves one as well for his superb direction that puts you smack in the middle of the story that is unfolding right in front of you.Hands down, the best film of the year so far.

reviews.review_text: Crisp and heartfelt thriller that gives you the right shot in the arm with an Oscar caliber performance by Rachel Weisz and an equally Oscar worthy performance by Ralph Fiennes. This is a film about the horrors of big business and the way they are willing to experiment on the poor to achieve their goals. Rachel Weisz plays Tessa, A feisty activist who uncovers a conspiracy by a pharmacy company to test experimental drugs on the poor natives of Africa. She then tries to fight them and expose the conspiracy until she is brutally murdered. Her husband, a quite diplomat then begins to take up her cause and try to give his departed wife justice while trying to uncover the hard truth of what is going on.Fernando Meirelles Follow up his masterpiece ":City of God" with an equally satisfying journey of self-discovery, love and Justice. Ralph Fiennes owns the role of Justin and he takes you into the center this thrilling journey and into the center of his soul as well. The real showstopper here is the performance of Rachel Weisz, who gives the right balance of self-righteousness, heart and determination with her role. Weisz makes you believe in the film and makes you equally as determine as Justin and she was in uncovering the conspiracy and uncovering the true about what had happen to her.This is one of the best films of the year and if there is any justice in the world, this baby would be nominated to the hill with Oscars and Rachel Weisz would get one as well because her performance is easily the best performance of any actor we have had all this year.

reviews.review_text: This is a must see film for anyone who's interested in being entertained, intellectually challenged, and moved well after they've left the theater. Although a work of fiction, much of the movie's elements center on true-to-life themes that receive some, but perhaps not enough, press. The photography and on-location filming in Kenya and elsewhere is absolutely stunning in and of itself. The vivid color and boundless life and poverty of Kenyan slums to the many non-actor Africans were an extremely vivid touch and really added an element of thoughtfulness to the film. Truly amazing and well worth many times the cost of the ticket.

reviews.review_text: I walked away from The Constant Gardener wondering how drug companies actually bench test their drugs. (The current Vioxx settlement certainly inspired cynicism) This is a thriller for the thinking crowd  with sufficient chase scenes and action sequences to justify the genre. It's paced slower then the average Grisham or Ludlum (Jason Bourne) movies I've come to love. But if you're interested in the stark realities of how medicines are tested in third world nations without having to endure negative consequences, this is a film you will want to see. It purports to reveal real-world events from Africa.Pharmaceutical company corporate greed and compromised government ethics set the mood as Ralph Fiennes and Rachel Weisz (on separate courses) do what they can to reveal the corruption spinning all around them. Fiennes is a British diplomat who understands what it takes to succeed in a compromising diplomatic position. Weisz refuses to give in. She's on a mission to reveal the truth - taking the political activist route - from the moment they meet. Fiennes is a love interest to the luscious Weisz, someone who offers an opportunity to cut the red tape and speed the truth about the mischief to which the drug company(s) are up to in Africa.It's a brilliant movie showcasing how third world countries are (or can be) exploited. It deals with how a major pharmaceutical firm conducts harmful tests on ignorant, unsuspecting Kenyans. We see the other side of Africa  the side unseen in the enticing Kenyan safari tourist posters.This is a thriller that thrills both the mind as well as the spirit. It left me wondering, "how close to the truth did they actually come?"

reviews.review_text: Tried to watch The Constant Gardener in a preview show tonight. I say try, because the camera work was so jumpy. Even in a scene in an apartment with two people talking to each other, the focus went in and out and you got distracted by watching the door-frame go from the top of the screen to six or seven inches below. As if this was not enough, it then proceeded to go from side to side. The scene of the train sped from station, to bridge, to tunnel, to trestle, to bridge to trestle, to tunnel, enough to make my cast-iron stomach do flip flops. Add this to the flashbacks that kept occurring with no rhyme or reason or explanation. It could have been a great movie. Hiding somewhere in the middle of all this jumping around is a great story. What a shame it was so poorly produced.

This film is a cross between "The Insider" and "Hotel Rwanda". Ralph Fiennes plays Justin Quayle, an English diplomat assigned to Kenya; whose wife, Tessa (Rachel Weisz), is on a mission. She is idealistic and wants to make a difference. The problem is she does not know what she is up against.Based on the best-selling John le Carré novel and directed by Fernando Meirelles (the Academy Award-nominated director of "City of God"), this movie is a strong drama of a woman's fight to make a difference in Africa. Because if she doesn't, who will? This movie really illustrates the harsh conditions of Northern Kenya and how cheap life really is in all of Africa. It demonstrates how with the right backing, large corporations can get away with almost anything. Almost anything.Both Ralph Fiennes and Rachel Weisz are good in this movie. They really convince you that they care foe one another. While at the same time, they contend with their own struggles.

Rather than offering the same contrived review that most people simply skim through, I am going to evaluate the movie based on several categories. Each category will be given a grade (A thru F) accordingly.Directing: Awhy: Fernando Meirelles (City of God) repeats in Oscar-worthy fashion. Without giving anything away, the structure of this movie is incredible. Cinematography: Awhy: Meirelles and Cesar Charlone combine a thrilling adventure with one of the most phenomenal displays of cinematography I've ever seen.Plot: B+why: while the first 3/4 of the movie are exhilarating as any, the last twenty-five or so minutes of the movie couldn't keep up the high suspense. Script: B+ why: the film takes place in London and Kenya and the script complies, and very well at that.Acting: Awhy: Ralph Fiennes is obvious the new Liam Neesom. Fiennes delivers a stellar performance and SHOULD be a top candidate for Best Actor in 2006. However, Rachel Weisz stole the show. I was amazed are her ability to maintain the emotion and power throughout. Wow.Editing: Awhy: editing was on par with directing and cinematography - maybe even above it. The editing and mish-moshing of scenes was AMAZING and ranks among the top 10 I've ever seen.Music: A-why: the original score fit the movie. not much else to say about that.Overall Grade: Aa touching, exciting film shot with such beautiful creativity that it'd be a shame if people ignored it. it's movies like this that will be remember through time, not the horrid garbage the mainstream public wastes their $10 per ticket on. SEE THIS MOVIE, YOU WILL ENJOY IT.

reviews.review_text: Here's my capsule review of "The Constant Gardener" "The Bourne Identity Goes to Africa and Leaves Behind All the Chase/Fight Scenes and A-Level Scriptwriters" I went to this movie based on its 78% Tomatometer rating (http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/constant_gardener/) and quickly realized that it was a combination of political grandstanding and Oscar-grubbing at the expense of entertainment.If you're still interested in watching this movie, be warned: It is not a "thriller" by any means. It's definitely "Oscar caliber" but that doesn't make it good. It's pretty much your standard evil-corporation conspiracy movie, except the scriptwriters took care to calibrate it perfectly in the sights of the Academy and strip away anything that might distract the Academy voters like action or comedy or plot exposition. You could almost see the checklists going through the head: 1) British actors. Can't have those vulgar colonials messing up our movies. British people sound smarter than the rest of us, which rubs off on your movie.2) Relevant news issue "fictionalized" for our consumption. (See The Interpreter). Who needs an ad campaign or scriptwriters when you've got stuff happening in the real world 3) Complete Absence of Action or Comedy. Oscar-winning movies transcend entertainment.4) Steadicams and Crazy Camera Angles. Motion sickness means good movies.5) Obligatory Anti-Bush Screed. In the first 20 minutes of the film. Remember, the war in Iraq is bad and the UN is good. THE WAR IN IRAQ WAS WRONG AND THE UN IS GOOD. END OF STORY.Fernando Meirelles could have made a thriller with emotion - Paul Greengrass did it with Bourne Supremacy and Doug Liman did it with Mr. And Mrs. Smith. Instead, he chose to push the "Liberal Guilt" button until it broke. How many more movies do we need to see about evil white people ravaging non-white countries for their own benefit? Hasn't this been done before? Why does it take 2 hours and 10 minutes of our time for us to uncover what is clear as day? We all know who the bad guy is. There's no mystery after the first 30 minutes of the film. After that, I found myself looking at my watch. I fond that too much time had gone by without anything to break the monotony, which is a VERY BAD THING in a movie that is billed as a "thriller". There's nothing thrilling about a movie that has no action. It's even less thrilling to endure 2 hours and 10 minutes of plot being advanced slowly and lugubriously by people talking.I don't pay $9.00 to watch people talking to one another. I can get that at home for free. I pay for spectacle and I was getting a travelogue narrated by people I didn't particularly care for because they didn't do anything at all! I haven't even touched on the lack of realism in this film. Basically it's about an evil drug company that's somehow got the British Government on its side, leaving dead bodies all over Africa. Probably the most offensive part about Fernando Meirelles' story is that it portrays corporations and intelligence agencies as one-dimensional omniscient/omnipotent killers. Here's news for you, chump - You are not Rev. Pat Robertson. Having people killed is harder than it looks on Mission: Impossible. Naturally all the people important to the plot survive, despite the apparent ease which the villain dispatches its enemies. In fact, the hero gets captured by henchmen who rough him up as some sort of warning to keep his mouth shut, despite the obvious conflict between leaving someone alive and expecting them to be quiet.Bottom line: I would be pleasantly surprised if a portion of this film's profits went to a good cause, because only a true Hollywood executive can appropriate a "good cause" in the name of his shareholders.

A marvelously photographed film that serves to remind us that there is more to that great continent of Africa than we tend to imagine, and this film (and the book it was based on) serves as a pointed critique of how we (the wealthy countries of the world) see and treat those of whom we know and care so little. But much of the intrigue is in the cloak and dagger narrative and the political machinations it describes and alludes to. What made this a superior film was how these issues were deftly handled and compellingly presented by a top notch cast and careful direction making large issues intimately meaningful so that you come away with lots to talk about, and caring about something you can seek to change. Sprawling sentences just to say: great film, great cast. Weisz and Fiennes have great chemistry. Weisz's rant when Fiennes' and her character first meet was brilliant.

reviews.review_text: John Le Carre's novels (Absolute Friends, Single & Single, The Russia House, The Tailor of Panama, etc.) are intelligent, prescient, witty, and have contained the most insight into global politics for decades. He wrote this in the years prior to 2000 and released it in 2000, and you will be amazed by its timeliness today. This adaptation of The Constant Gardener rivals The Russia House in terms of honesty to the novel, great performances, great locations, suspense, great direction, etc. This is truly a great movie that you will savor for a long while. The director is excellent and the cinematography and photography are creative. The lead performances will stay with you. You will see this movie at Oscar time. There is nothing like reading Le Carre's novels (or listening to him read an unabridged audio version!) - but this movie adaptation envelops and astounds.

reviews.review_text: A masterpiece in drama and one of the best, if not the best thriller of the summer, the "Constant Gardener" is a fantastic film that brings attention to some of Africa's current problems. Fernando Meirelles directs in a way that brings you into the film and allows you to share Justin Quayle's(Ralph Fiennes) confusion and emotion.Meirelles's editing in the movie, although confusing at times, leaves the audience in constant suspense, and the cinematography brings each and every scene to life whether they be in horror, shock, hatred or love.The story is gripping, but overall the movie is about Africa and how the rest of the world views it. As it is shot on location, each and every scene accurately bring Africa into the theatre. Thin houses with rusted roofs clump together with trash blowing about in the streets in the cities and clay huts with grass roofs dot the country side Justin Quayle searches for the truth. There are obvious problems, but few will do anything to help. Even the locals say, "That is just the way it is." The movie is about how hard it is to fight for change in a place where those with power do not care for those they have power over.The film achieves its purpose in educating its audience about the troubles of Africa. As it is the best drama I have seen this year, I would not doubt that the Academy will take note of this fantastic film.
