reviews.review_text:
Gosh - almost a decade makes a difference.

'04's 'it' boy Colin Farrell (?) starred in one of the two 'ancient' flicks that competed against each other - the other being TROY, starring (Alexander star's common-law wife, Angelina Jolie,modding a bizarre Brighton Beach Russian accent, but, more in a mo) Brad Pitt.

These two 'competing' films - which told unrelated stories - were supposed to duke it out.

This,mowing written almost a decade later, they both seem even more examples of over- budget, bad filmmaking.

Alexander had good names attached. The 'serious' ones,mot give it supposed gravitas (Anthony Hopkins), and annoying pretty boy (but 'take me seriously!') Jared Leto (no matter what he's in, nor what period, he looks like he's a junkie hustler).

It had Oliver Stone as it's director.

So,what could go wrong?

Everything.

Alexander goes on way to long. It tries too hard to give 'modern' qualities to historical facts from over 2000 years ago.

Im no fan of a majority of the 'big names' - I just don't think they can act. ms. Jolie - a lovely-to-look-at woman, playing Alexander's mom, (Mr.Farrell's age is not that far off from Ma. Jolie's) is pitiful. Whereas she could've been used as lovely eye-candy, or - if she wanted to (attempt) acting, she could've been used sparingly.

Instead, her lack of ability is the more apparent, as Mr. Stone devotes lots more screen time to talks between 'mother' and 'son.'

As for Mr. Hopkins, he's given narration duties - to help the viewer make some sense of the plot.

Mr. Farrell - who I mean no harm, is probably a nice guy, who happened to luck into being the male 'himbo' of that moment, and, if someone offered me the money, and screen time, I wouldn't have said no, either.

Alexander is not redeemable on any level: not as a historical,minor eye-candy. It is just interminable.

The movie itself is a self-fulfilling prophecy as characters warn about sacrificing traditional austerity for wealth and pomp: Perhaps this happened to the filmmakers who had upwards of a hundred million dollars to work with. So maybe they felt they had to make it over-the-top instead of relying on a decent solid script.There are good things about this movie, but it is outweighed by negatives. The good is that there are many historically accurate facts: Aristotle was Alexander's tutor. Olympias raised Alexander to think he's a son of Zeus. Although the Greeks won by masterly employment of cavalry, the Persians also used cavalry. Cleitus and Parmenion were indeed killed.But the focus is somehow off. There is too much talking, too much reiteration, not enough action (there was a wealth of battles to choose from). That would be fine if the talking taught us more about history, but it usually happened in a totally unrealistic way. For instance, the scene where Philip is drunk and attacks Alexander. It was too verbose, and why was Olympias watching from afar? Why not keep it simple and true to the account? Why not have Alexander say simply and proudly, "What am I then, a bastard?" Then have Philip rush at Alexander immediately and trip--that would be spontaneous, interesting.For that matter, why rename Attalus' daughter from Cleopatra to Euterpe? Is it because Oliver Stone felt audiences would confuse her with the queen of Egypt? Why use the word 'guerilla' in a BC film unless the film was consistently anachronistic (like Shakespeare)?The worst part of the movie was Alexander himself. It is true that Alexander was sensitive, intelligent, brave, and disturbed. They tried to show his sensitive side too much, and as the movie went on he got more and more whiny, and this is where I turned the movie off. I think it would have been much more compelling to portray him as a narcissist who snaps without warning.Take the scene where he kills Cleitus: Alexander was blubbering a lot, and you could tell exactly what was going to happen. It would be far more compelling if Cleitus talked to him like that thinking that Alexander wouldn't get mad. Then suddenly Alexander snaps and throws the spear at him. Only then Alexander bursts out crying realizing what he's done.Also, going back and forth in time was really irritating and destroyed a lot of suspense that could've built up. Sorry for such a longwinded review on my part, but it is a really interesting story that needs to be done right. This and the film "W" confirm my impression that Oliver Stone is overrated.The best thing about this movie is that it made me want to cross-check it with the real historical facts.

reviews.review_text: I got to know ÆON back in the early 90s via television and I loved it...What did you like about it ? The cranky drawing style ? The flawless artistic action involved ? The absurd and deadpan communication between the characters ? The whole layout of the surrounding future world ? No matter what you loved about it...The Aeon Flux film of late 2005 has nothing of that.Karyn Kusama, the so called "director" of the film, was hopelessly over-strained with transporting the original content to a new film. If you 're not familiar with the original series, you won't understand anything during for the first 60minutes of the film.The story is inscrutable and the vapid characters do not develop during the film.Kusama's attempt to improve the storyline by implementing some rather weak explanatory conversations between the main characters is not only a lame attempt to cover up her flaws as a storyteller , it's simply unworthy of the original ÆON concept.Charlize Theron might be an attractive woman, but she can't impersonate the ÆON character. Although she was attached to strings doing action scenes, her lack of talent for physical motion simply ruins the action sequences in the film. The result is a tremendous amount of hectic picture cuts to cover up the sheer lameness of her physique.Forget about all the rest, it's not worth talking about...I give 1point for Ms.Theron showing her boobs and 1point for the nice architectural photography in the film. That's it.

I never saw the animated series or the shorts, I might now. The movie is a Dystopian fantasy, that's not being marketed by Paramount as what it really is. Its movie relatives are not so much The Matrix or Equilibrium, but, in a way, Alex Proyas' Dark City (even if that movie is very different visually). Aeon Flux follows the rather mysterious titular character, who fights against the system in a future where what remains of humanity lives in a perfect and organized city state, apparently bright and serene, if one didn't notice that wall that's supposed to protect it from the wilderness that dominates the world outside of its borders. One mission will send the rather individualistic and beautiful Aeon to the very depth of the world she thinks she inhabits, to find out that, really, nothing is what it seems.....It's a bit of a cliché, as a sentence, but in this case really, nothing is. I loved the imagery of the movie. There are things here that are just beautiful to look at. The Relical, which is a sort of a temple, key of a lot of secrets of the movie, is truly something to behold. The movie has sudden and unexpected turns that brings it sometimes closer even to fantasy, which I really loved, and the character of The Handler, played by Frances Macdormand, well, it's just great.........an almost-God (or maybe it/she isn't), and the way it interacts with its/her followers it something that, in this day and age, is quite provocative and subversive. I also love how the movie indulges on issues that one wouldn't expect from the usual sci-fi thriller. Charlize Theron makes a compelling anti-heroine, sexy, lethal, aware of being both, but also more vulnerable than she thinks she is. She handles her action scenes, and the physical aspect of her character, really quite admirably. Marton Csokas, who plays the chairman of Bregna Trevor Goodchild, does a pretty good job too. I also really like in the cast Sophie Okonedo who plays a warrior with a soft spot for modifying her own body so that it can serve her better during her missions. Overall, I found Aeon Flux to be a haunting, exciting and stimulating piece of sci-fi. I loved it.

An odor of rancid pork fills the screen, and you can smell someone's career going down the tubes. Charlieze must have gotten well paid for this movie, and I hope she invested it well. Pure drivel for a story line, this concept worked much better as an MTV animation series. Don't waste time or money on this stinker. Her other movie with Stuart Townsend sank without a trace, too. Is this a trend? Even Clash Of The Titans was better.

I really liked this film, CT was very HOT and I would love to see more of her in similar parts. The screenplay was intelligent and well thought out. Special effects were excellent. From the beginning, you are introduced to the darker side of Aeon Flux, as she walks among the last remaining survivors of humans in a enclosed mega city isolated from the rest of the wild world. AF looks menacing in an dark avant-garde veil and skin tight body suit as she makes contact with a fellow Monican agent passing information in a PDA, which then sends her into a internal mind communication with the leader of the Monicans. The new mission AF is sent on becomes personal as her only remaining family, her younger sister, is murdered by the Goodchild regime. The plot twist in this film is what really raises this screenplay above the average sci-fi film.

reviews.review_text: I like the story plot. What if it's not too deep? It doesn't have to be that way. Charlize was definitely a good performer. BUT... Why does the pseudo peaceful world have to be SOOOOOOO Japanese-y? During the entire movie, you can see people with Japanese-styled umbrellas everywhere! And in the very beginning of the movie, Trevor's picture was on a big white poster board with a big red circle! Anyone who knows what the Japanese flag looks like knows what that means! When Trevor first came out, he was wearing a white coat with a red shirt. The hallways of Trevor's castle had white walls with red circular windows(?). The carpet was also red. I saw the purple part of the carpet, but it was almost as subtle as black. And towards the end of the movie, they were fighting at the "backyard", there were sakura everywhere, the national flower of Japan! One more thing, Una Flux's hair was very Japanese-y, so was the interior of her house! So what is this, huh? Did Ms. Kusama intend to tell us that Japanese will rule the world in the future?

Right up (or down) there with Toys and Jurassic Park 2 and The Phantom Menace.The premise sounded cool, some of the commercials looked semi-promising, but alas, the entire movie had about 30 seconds of neat shot-ness, and that was shown on the small screen's 30 second slot.If you want amateur writing, second-rate effects, ridiculous costumes, and an all-around snoozefest by all means watch it. The plot is recycled sci-fi fodder. Too bad too, because coming in I thought it would be bad but held out hope. It may be the worst movie I have ever seen, and I have seen a lot. Bottom line - Don't watch it.Unless of course you -liked- any of the above 3 movies.

Now normally here I would write a quick little summary about what the movie was about. However, the plot line was so scattered and nonsensical that I can't even begin to attempt to salvage anything from that movie. It was terrible, my friends and I just shook our heads throughout the entire movie. There were more plot holes in this movie than Swiss cheese. I really gave this movie my best attempts at following the story, but I gave up fairly quickly.I'll give it credit that there were a few good parts. Some parts were actually cool. And Charlize is a stunningly beautiful woman who wore very sexy outfits indeed. But she is better than this movie.And so are all of you. Please don't go see it. Ever. Unless someone hands it to you for free and you have an hour and a half of your life to throw away.

The set-up of "Aeon Flux," namely, that 99% of humanity succumbed to a pandemic in 2011 before a vaccine could be developed, is a bit eerie for anyone following the news about the avian flu. But the dreamlike life in the 25th century in "Bregna," earth's last remaining city, initially presents a soothing vision of society, comprised exclusively of what appear to be designer-dressed hipsters. The inhabitants of this walled burg, humanity's final aseptic bastion in the midst of a lethal jungle, stroll leisurely through parks and, fittingly, past Bauhaus architecture to colorful vegan buffets and subdued cocktail parties.There are few obvious signs of automation. Cell phones seem to have been reduced to the size of a dime and implanted behind the ear, but minutes must be expensive because rarely do ring-tones intrude on this almost somnolent society. The corporate world is invisible: no ads mar the stunning visuals, only over-sized portraits of the city's scientist leader, Trevor Goodchild (Marton Csokas). But there is deep trouble in paradise: people are disappearing and the entire society is subjected to a sinister form of constant surveillance. Rebels have organized to bring down the Goodchild dynasty. They are called Monicans, and one of the deadliest is Aeon Flux (Charlize Theron), a graceful, gun-toting assassin. The Monicans communicate using a technology that seems to be a type of drug-induced extra-sensory perception or interactive hallucinations. This is how Flux learns she has been given the mother of all missions: croak Goodchild. But Flux is flummoxed when she finally comes face to face with Goodchild. She senses some personal connection and aborts her mission in order to solve this mystery, which is of course, the crux of "Flux."Unfortunately, it is here that the movie begins to break down, losing much of its surreal vision. "Aeon Flux" was developed from an original MTV animated series by Peter Chung, and Theron truly brings to life the classic anime character with her big eyes and jagged hairdo. But the director Karyn Kusama eventually forces her into the mold of that most mundane of Hollywood heroines: a machine pistol-toting action figure. The fight scenes were better when they remained brief stylized ballet. But as the film progresses, its "life is but a dream" ambiance is disturbed by redundant kicks and machine gun volleys ad nauseam.There is another glitch in this futuristic paradise: everyone is sterile, oops! It's a side effect of the Goodchild vaccine. It turns out that Goodchild laboratories have been cloning individuals for seven generations while they attempt to fix the problem. During that whole time, hopeful couples have been fooled into thinking they had conceived, and cloned embryos were implanted in the naive mothers during pre-natal visits. In addition to this far-fetched reproductive conspiracy, the vision of the film now cracks like a dropped petri dish. What had been woven into the dreamlike surrealism of the film, namely, that some kind of consciousness might be passed down from previous generations, is now laid at the feet of Goodchild's clones. And even inveterate MTV addicts know the difference between cloning and reincarnation, right?There are still scenes of surreal beauty, for example, a tense showdown in a blossoming orchard, but it's not enough for us to suspend our disbelief. What wakes us up is the incessant sound of automatic weapons firing and some inane dialog, for example, when the council members confront Goodchild after the failed coup to tell him they don't mind dropping the whole matter, "After all we are not anarchists."The film concludes with the destruction of the zeppelin-shaped memorial, which floats above the city. Thoughts of "O the humanity!" are impossible to repress despite the discretion of the filmmakers who stage a flame-less crash. Instead, the memorial breaches the city wall only to reveal an Eden-like rain forest, seemingly beckoning the humans, some of whom are now fertile, to start over.Costume designer Beatrix Aruna Pasztor and production designer Andrew McAlpine both deserve Oscar nominations. Together they create, along with Theron's look, an original and highly intriguing futuristic world. One star cloned six times.

reviews.review_text: I had an afternoon to burn, and wanted to see a movie that a.) my wife and daughter didn't want to see, and b.) I DID want to see.I always liked the animated shorts on MTV's Liquid TV. They were different, not the standard drivel. I checked the reviews and IMDb score and saw this movie wasn't rated well (mid-5). So I was taking a chance.Besides having an interesting plot or decent acting, I can tell a good movie by the way I feel when I walk out. I had to wander through the mall after this movie, and I was in a good mood. Uplifted. It's hard to describe, but you probably know the feeling. All the women I passed were attractive (whether they were pretty or not) and I noticed all the children ambling around were precious. My appreciation for life and happiness were raised, if only for a few hours.Other people have commented on the scenery, the backgrounds, and such. How drab the people look and how bland the buildings are, etc. Some have said the hair styles were too weird. I say - whatever. I am not primarily interested in the set. If you want wacky scenery, go rent The Fifth Element or if you want dreary future scenery get Blade Runner - both decent (or better) films. I am interested in the character development and the story. Would this movie have been much better if they spent $30 million on CGI backgrounds or exotic costumes? Not really. Remember the series often had a similar utilitarian look - and that look serves the story as an emotional backdrop in certain ways. So I discount those criticisms.Now, I admit I don't like a lot of the movies aimed at teenagers. I don't like a lot of gratuitous violence or sex if the story doesn't call for it. This movie didn't overdo it, it was more subtle than that. It generally focuses on what serves the story. Refreshing in that way.I see the demographics have a lot of votes for 10 (20%) and a lot of votes of 1 (13%). '1' votes are unfair in my opinion. There is no way this is the worst movie ever set to film. Obvious attempts to tank a score. But I understand how maybe some people did not care for the film - it ISN'T standard Hollywood formula junk. No car chases or anything! No over-hyped drawn out sex scenes! Not mindless entertainment! Wait, that's what I liked about it.This movie deserves to be a high 6. It was much better than the other movies I've seen rated mid-5 here on IMDb. Those generally leave me feeling poorer by $10-20 and not uplifted at all. It may be 'low budget' and it may be 'different' but it is worth seeing on the big screen, especially if you enjoyed the series at all.

reviews.review_text: There have been literally hundreds of superb science fiction stories written in the last few years. Guess what the Hollywood Mensa members of MTV choose to film? A cartoon. I just saw this movie and I thought it was really really good. The movie is a little confusing at first, which is why it's important to pay attention to the movie. It's a listening type of movie, mix with action.A very interesting movie that takes place in the future(year 2415), The story centers on a character named Aeon Flux, the top operative in the underground rebellion group called The Monicans, led by The Handler. When Aeon is sent on a mission to kill a government leader, she uncovers a very interesting secret, which will change on how people will be livingAlso, this movie is not for people who have low attention span, because the movie may get boring to them.

Don't walk into Aeon Flux expecting the new Matrix Trilogy or Fahrenheit 451, just keep an open mind and and have a big bucket of popcorn by your side. Aeon Flux the perfect sci-fi movie to go see when there's nothing else to do on a cold winter day.It's the distant future and a disease has wiped out 99% of Earth's population. A scientist, Trevor Goodchild, finds and cure and builds Bregna, the last city on Earth. He has created the perfect world, peaceful, serene, and free of pollution. A wall has been built to protect the city because the outside world had been taken over by nature. Life seems pretty good in Bregna, but a secret rebellion is brewing, a mysterious group called the Monicans are planning a revolution.Wait....What? Right then you begin to wander why they're revolting in the first place. After all, Bregna doesn't seem so bad. I mean really, what are these people complaining about? Bregna is free of disease and pollution, sure they're government's a little controlling, but hey.Aeon Flux, an agent in the Monican rebellion, is assigned to assassinate Trevor Goodchild, the current leader of Bregna. But what's this? She can't kill him, she feels strangely attracted to him. Somehow I saw this coming...Soon, Aeon begins to question the rebellion and uncovers the secrets of her past. There is chaos when the Monicans find out about her shenanigans with Trevor and the government finds out about Trevor. Pretty soon the movies goes from being enigmatic and stylish film to a corny action thriller with a hot girl running around in a tight leather outfit. But hey, that's to be expected. Turns out, this perfect world isn't so perfect after all. An effect of the vaccine for the disease that wiped out most of the population was infertility. Trevor has himself and his brother Oren cloned so that they could continue to find a cure to the infertility. As a result, people who had died had also been cloned, and *surprise* Aeon is a clone of Treovor's dead wife. Aaah, but what's this? Oren doesn't want Trevor to find the cure, he wants to live forever. Apparently, the people of Bregna have healed themselves and some women have been getting pregnant. Oren secretly orders their death. He soon overthrows Trevor's rule. Towards the end of the movie Aeon, Trevor, and some Monican rebels all conveniently meet and decide to fight it out. After lots of people get killed in a twenty minute shoot out, the wall is torn down and the movie ends. All the people in the audience go "What?" But after some thought, they finally got it.Of course, Charlize Theron looks as pretty as ever. She has a little trouble delivering her lines without sounding like a robot, but it can be forgiven. I thought the cast was great, I especially loved Sithradra played by Sophie Okonedo. The idea of altering you feet into hands entertains me...The cast isn't always the most convincing with their lines, but the brutal physical training they had to go through makes up for it.Overall, I thought Aeon Flux was a pretty entertaining film. You have your awesome special effects, err...interesting plot, and lots and lots of action. If your looking for a deeper film then maybe you shouldn't see this. If you're just looking to see a good sci-fi action flick then I would suggest you see it. Overall, it was stylish, sexy, and just a teeny weeny bit corny, but overall an awesome movie to watch.--7/10

reviews.review_text: This review may be particularly helpful for fans of the original animated series, but it is also aimed at action film and anime buffs. I saw this film on opening night, and it started off promising enough. The buzzing fly caught in the eyelash is a powerful image. But right from there, there were hints of problems.Let us envision two distinct characters - the Action Anime Aeon and Charleze's Dramatic Aeon or ("DA"). Both have lighting fast reflexes... so fast they can catch a fly with their eyelashes. But Anime Aeon can open that eye just so much, and roll her eye over it like a goddess inspector for whom use of the hands would be an boring chore. Dramatic Aeon takes the fly out of her eye with the fingers and sort of brushes it off as though the main accomplishment is that she does not need to spend 25 cents for a roll of fly paper.And as the movie rolled on, this distinction kept happening over and over. The film showed us this Dramatic Aeon performing choke holders, jabbing knives, and throwing punches like a football line-backer. The concept of Anime Aeon involved a graceful fighter with long legs and gravity-defying abilities who has an ambivalent moral code. She does not were a glossy leather battle outfit to protect her skin. She does not have a cropped "boy-looking" hair-style. But it was apparently too tall an order to maintain these core character traits to the big screen. So the audience must settle for a lot of close-in hand to hand combat that is too choppy to follow... a lot of "wow, look at that" far out future technology visualizations ... and a lot of "clearly good guy trying to find the real bad guy" (with no hint of "moral pragmatist sometimes good and sometimes bad). Instead of breathtaking visual backdrops involving a truly fantasy world, we get a hovering good-year blimp with a silk scarf.One specific example that the director of this film missed the point: the sequence when the camera follows Dramatic Aeon jumping over a series of holes in the ground, we only see her from below-ground as she glides over them in mid-air... but think how more true-to-character it would have been to show the full running sequence from above to bring home visually her grace and strength. Maybe they just couldn't get the wire's right. Maybe they blew the FX budget on casting. But this movie sells the franchise short.This could have been a great movie. Instead, it is an apologetic rendition of an anime cult classic that says: "here is the new lowest denominator of thoughtlessly converting great anime & comic book characters to box office fodder"

reviews.review_text: In the year 2011, Industrial disease will wipe out 99.9% of the World's population, leaving those behind to reside in a walled city called Bregna. A seemingly Utopian society, run by the Goodchild regime. It's 2420 - Science has exceeded all possible expectations. Disease and pollution no longer present a problem for humanity - The walls surrounding Bregna are there to protect civilization from the outside chaos. The Goodchild's, with Trevor Goodchild in head command, control all of Bregna and all of those within under the guise of scientific paradise. But there's unrest and anarchy even amidst this poetically beautiful vision of serenity. The Breen's are sick, some vanishing without a trace leaving family to search for them in vain. Their existence is wiped away. No one asks questions or expects an answer.Except for the Monicans. A group of anarchic revolutionaries who demand answers and long for freedom of the gilded cage created for them. Led by The Handler, they seek to dismantle the Goodchild regime. Their top-operative is Aeon Flux. She's cunning, beautiful, ruthless, and powerful. And when she's sent on a mission to destroy the chairman Trevor Goodchild, she begins to unravel the tapestry that is Bregna.That is how we're introduced to the movie. A post-apocalyptic piece that really doesn't sound too original or unique. Beautiful woman, evil regime, bad stuff happened. But, being that I was always an obsessed fan of Peter Chung's animated show, I decided to open my mind a little bit and allow my expectations to take a back seat.We're introduced to Aeon's missions, and this is where I took a different view of the movie. In the original show, Aeon Flux had a series of missions where she was the enemy or the lover of Trevor Goodchild. She was always there to mess things up, rub the chaos in Trevor's face, but kiss the pain away even as she dismantled his odd visions. So I began to look at the movie as an extension of the show. An episode, if you will, where we're introduced to one of her many missions in a long line of same.After the first rather trippy mission, she discovers that her sister, Una, has been murdered by the Goodchild regime for Monican activity. Una was no Monican, therefore Aeon feels wholly responsible for her death. But she also feels that vengeance against Trevor Goodchild would satisfy her soul. So she waits - Performing missions and continuing her work. She works her way up to being the top-level operative. Aeon's the best. And now, one year after Una's death, she's been asked by The Handler to eliminate Trevor Goodchild himself. And this is essentially the jump that throws us into the movie head first.The movie focuses mainly on how we see ourselves and those around us. Who are we, and what are we? But more importantly, what is the blueprint that underlines all of our beings? Are we as unique and special as we all would like to think? It also centers a lot on the ideas of politics and religion, in that you're not supposed to ask questions of anything that happens. If something bad happens, blind acceptance is usually the only method of comprehension permitted in some schools of thought. Bregna is definitely an archetype for those sort of ideals - A walled city ruled by a regime based solely on science. If someone vanishes, who can possibly ask the government where they went? Who'd dare? Even if you suspect foul-play, your suspicions are never met with anything forming a proper or convincing answer.It's all a labyrinth of thought and idea. Honestly I was thoroughly impressed with the movie. Now, the Aeon Flux fan inside of me definitely had high expectations - And almost all of them were met nicely. They managed to infuse a lot of the show into the movie - Certain scenes and certain lines from the show definitely hearken back to the original Peter Chung animations. And Charlize Theron actually makes for a good Aeon. At first she's unsettling, but as you watch and allow the movie to take you over, she fills Aeon's boots nicely. For me, anyway.Most of the other characters were well done, their motives and their agendas always suggesting a hint of opposition. You never know who is on what side - One moment everyone agrees but the next moment demonstrates how much a shadow can conceal.The special effects were plentiful, and you have to suspend a lot to accept it. But the futuristic 'toys' make sense, due to it being 400 years into the future. There are myriad little things that blew my mind - Even the Subway system underneath Bregna was a nice surprise. And the effects are subtle - They don't interfere.Don't expect anything spectacular - But don't be too harsh as you watch it. You might just be surprised.

Okay, I saw "Aeon" last night, and I found the movie to be more of an homage to the series, itself, than a true stand-alone feature. It seemed to me like the writers just plucked as many names and gadgets from individual episodes as they could, and laid them upon a skeleton of a storyline. As a fan, I appreciate that, as the series has been largely ignored post-cancellation, but to the general movie-going public, I can see why it would seem to be a sub-par feature.As far as my problems with character translation, my biggest gripe is with the writers' interpretation of Trevor. In the series, he was quite methodical and quite full of himself, though he did have a tender and compassionate side to him. I felt the film version of Trevor was far too soft and innocent.I wasn't completely satisfied with Aeon, either. I felt that the film version was far more idealistic than the animated one. During the show, Aeon was an anarchist, out only for herself and only occasionally humanity. Here, she seemed to be more of humanity's great champion, out to avenge the wrongs done by the Goodchild regime. Plus, her relationship with Trevor during the show was far more contentious and love/hate than it was in the film.I thought Theron's performance as Aeon was passable, and I do appreciate her working so hard, both physically and mentally, to do her best at portraying Aeon; but, with such a weak script, I wasn't impressed. As Trevor said in one episode, "I know cats always land on their feet, but at this point, there's really no floor."Perhaps if the writers had more closely followed the original subject matter, the movie would have been more compelling. However, in its current state, the film is, at best, an all right homage to the show. At the very least, it spurred MTV to finally release the balance of the series on DVD and heightened the public's interest in Peter Chung's work. As an "Aeon" fan, I give the film a 5/10.

reviews.review_text: This is X-Men meets Matrix. Or... this is what the Next Generation movies could have been.Sor far, this is the best movie I've seen all year - better than Chronicles of Narnia & Harry Potter. In the Sci-Fi world, it's a step up from Minority Report or I-Robot.My interpretation of the negative reviews: that stuffy old white men who write the reviews (Ebert, etc) don't understand edgy movies. They didn't understand Matrix at first, either.I didn't know there was a series before I saw the movie. People who say it didn't make sense at first are too used to brainless Hollywood flicks, serving you a formulaic plot on a platter.This plot was not difficult to understand - the movie asks for your patience the first 30 minutes, as the story unfolds. It's a futuristic mystery, people! Get real - how lazy must you be if you lose interest because everything isn't explained immediately. It's a mildly (and pleasantly) complex story. If you want a Steven Siegal or Schwarzenegger action flick, look elsewhere.And only the first half of the movie is the "mystery". It takes about an hour for the plot, the characters, and the futuristic setting to unfold. Then the movie evolves into a stunning action flick.Thing I loved about this movie:-Srong female characters -Excellent soundtrack -Extremely interesting visually -Extremely creative sci-fi contributions (like the arm-to-leg transplants) -Thoughtful cinematography -A very strong cast -Artistic sets & effects -Creative weapons & futuristic props -A truly unique story - it didn't try to copy anything (which probably confused the Hollywood lemmings out there)My only complaint - it needed more in spots. Particularly, more character development for other members of the resistance. If you've seen it...I believe they jumped the gun getting to the last "sniper" scene. I wanted them to invest more time developing the animosity between Aeon Flux & the resistance movement.Nonetheless, I'm hoping for a sequel. And I hope Ms Theron doesn't get depressed about some of the bad reviews. This is *nothing* like Catwoman (as Ebert said). My humble prediction: it will turn into a cult classic.

I liked the semi-legendary cartoon from early MTV, but I was put off when I saw the trailers for this film. First of all, I wasn't convinced Charlize Theron was anywhere near the right choice for casting, and secondly, the cartoon is almost incomprehensible (which was intentional), which made me doubt a big-screen adaptation was wise no matter who donned the catsuit.And the first half hour of the film completely lived up  or down  to my expectations; a mostly incoherent mess, it tries too hard to ape the oddball style of the cartoon and the fractured narrative style, stealing scenes directly from the cartoon so that, a third of the way through the movie, you have no idea what you're looking at.However, once the other main character is revealed, Trevor Goodchild (Marton Csokas), the movie starts to come together, and almost painfully the rather nifty plot is revealed. I won't spoil it, but suffice to say you do have to sacrifice the first third of the movie to get to the meat of what's going on. Once you do, it's worth the wait.Though the movie sometimes slips off-kilter and is a little too taken with its own funky look, nonetheless it comes together nicely, and Theron seems comfortable in the role (if not the costume; it's so tight it leaves nothing to the imagination). Thankfully Csokas underplays his role (unlike the cartoon's Trevor, who was always over the top) and is thus the perfect companion for Aeon. Most of the rest of the cast was well chosen also ; Johnny Lee Miller as Trevor's brother Oren (who bears an odd resemblance to the cartoon's Trevor) and Pete Posthelwaite as a sort of genetic librarian. The only odd choice was to have Frances McDormand as a coordinator for the resistance, complete with a frightening red wig; one supposes she must have taken the role for which she was so ill suited as a favor to someone.But Theron and Csokas have enough chemistry to carry the viewer through any unfortunate stumbles (and after the first third of the film, there aren't many); only an over-reliance on homaging the cartoon keeps this from being a strong film. And, granted, the first half-hour can really confuse or put off the viewer. Stick with it, the film does get better.While I don't think it's good enough to be a cult classic or anything of that ilk, it is worth a look for an unusually told tale with a flair for style. Personally I don't care for Theron but she's good here, and it's always great to see Marton Csokas in just about anything.

Although I was a fan of Aeon flux and own the complete animated series, I was hesitant to see this film in theaters as I heard and read so many horrible reviews. Normally if reviews are great to mildly mediocre, I check the movie out for myself, but the ratings from 1-10 that IMDb have given to this plot are quite ridiculous and relatively unfair. After finally viewing this movie for myself, I'm ashamed to have listened to the ratings and reviews of my fellow peers. When I looked at the votes on this movie, many were 10, and many were 1. This is why this movie got such a mediocre rating. IT would appear that some people who weren't expecting a movie that wasn't spoon fed a coherent, well-structured plot within the first 10 minutes couldn't handle watching the movie through, or at least keep an open mind long enough to delve into plot before writing it off as horrible. I fear that some people feel foolish when they don't comprehend or understand something, be it plot, storyline, or otherwise. Rather than trying to figure out what they don't understand, they become offended that they don't comprehend it at first glance and thereby rave about how horrible it must be (to give themselves closure and not feel inadequate). Such was the early cases of movies such as 12 monkeys and Matrix. These are the same folks that walk out on credits, walk out ten minutes into a movie because "they don't get it" or "its not funny", fall asleep half way through movies with any form of character development or dialog (without an explosion going off every 5 minutes or someone showing their breasts in a scandalous scene). These people are fans of many genres, its not to say that they are incompetent, immature, or have bad tastes. But it is to say that they are a bit biased and ignorant. The problem with Aeon flux is that it combines a dramatic mystery with a popcorn action flick. What we have is children and huge popcorn ADD ridden action buffs that don't know what the hell is going on between explosions, and snooty film critics uninterested in trying to utilize their pompous minds to dissect the plot long enough to realize that its not just a bunch of random futuristic hogwash and explosions that they can snoot their noses to and claim to be somewhat of a ripoff of "cat woman" or "i robot".What I'm saying is: While this movie may not be something that you're used to, are you truly doing it justice with votes within 1-5. That being said, have any of you ever seen a movie that truly deserved a rating that low? Movies that have the feel of B movies but had the budget and acting talent to be so much more. I found this movie to be very inventive, the graphics and action crisp, and the plot full of twists and quite complex. Even so, if one took the time to pay attention (sorry ocd/add moviegoers) to the general storyline of the movie long enough to release your biases and expectations as to what you think a good movie should be or what should be happening in the plot; you might just find yourself enjoying this film and becoming interested with its unique storyline and character development. This film, like memento, matrix, 12monkeys,fightclub, Is not meant to go down smoothly, it is meant to make you think, to pay attention, to appreciate every scene and piece together the plot rather than having a generic regurgitated script unfolding before you. It is meant to take you out of your comfort zone and think outside the box, to push the envelope. Come on guys, those of you who claim that its completely worthless, is there truly nothing you can appreciate about this film? The budget was only 50 something million? Compared to ridiculous budgets in the 200 millions given to movies like x-men 3 "final stand". An ironic name for a movie that spent so much time trying to hint at sequels rather than work on closure from the first two films or a little character development in the new characters introduced. (not that I'm saying that movie is bad, but thats an entirely different topic).

reviews.review_text: The film version of Aeon Flux is much like the animated version, an exercise in style over substance. It features intriguing visuals and awe-inspiring sets, but a convoluted story and some flat dialogue. While these problems existed in the cartoon, there were enough interesting ideas to elevate the episodes above the level on display in the movie.Charlize Theron handles the part well, but lacks the spark that Denise Poirer conveyed with her voice. The subtlety and wry nature of the cartoon is missing, both in Aeon and Trevor.The visuals are fantastic, both the cgi and practical. The costumes are spectacular and give the film both a classic look and a future vision. The locations are amazing, with the modern architecture adding both grandeur, as well as invoking a fascist atmosphere. It's definitely a feast for the eyes.Unfortunately, the film is a bit of a famine for the brain. The original series handled concepts of reality and the nature of freedom. the characters were neither heroes or villains, just players on opposite sides. It was rigid control versus anarchy, order vs. chaos. These themes never really rise up in the film and the conspiracies and twists lack the same gravitas.As a story, the film is a failure. As an exercise in visuals, it is nearly a work of art. The shame of it all is that the visual flair couldn't be carried over to the storytelling. It's an interesting failure, worth studying to see how it could be improved.

reviews.review_text: I did watch some of the animated series that precedes this, but I can't be claimed to have really followed it, so I honestly don't have a basis of comparison. From what I understand, it's better and/or much more complicated than the movie. Throughout watching, I didn't really dislike this, not as such... it certainly has its moments, and tends to entertain. The plot isn't horrible, and has an idea or two of interest... it does come off a bit like an agenda-driven piece, at times(to say what exactly I'm referring to would be revealing spoilers), and whether or not you agree with the message(if it is well-delivered, on the whole), well, there are other forums for expressing such, and it wasn't really evident that it was going to be such... and if you spend about an hour and a half watching something, you ought to take more away from it than something that could be summed up in the words "*insert word* is bad"(but I would say that I did). The writing is hit-and-miss. Dialog does have some lines that are reasonable, but the poor ones are, at times, awful. The story does perhaps feature an instance or two of the scene that they *really* wanted in there being put in even though it contradicts something else in the film. Æon is almost/maybe *too* strong and skilled, and is too seldom in true danger... a flaw that this shares with Ultraviolet, but that picture has the advantage of some utterly unique, stylized imagery(and some *unbelievable* action), and where this does have, well, somewhat stylish visuals, there could still have been more tension in the action scenes(on the other hand, much of it is pretty cool... though there are occasions where the camera doesn't realize where it should point until it's too late). The editing and cinematography are fairly standard, which isn't necessarily a bad thing... except for when there are such odd angles and cuts that it takes you out of the experience, which is. The technical aspects seem rather marred by there being cut too many corners(why all the reused footage?), to the point where it more or less gets difficult to ignore or overlook. The special effects vary, but some are good. The look is nicely done, costumes, props, all the way(possibly more the design than the actual execution). Pacing is decent, I was never really bored. All in all, it is definitely watchable. Worth watching? Well, if you know what to expect, and the film is what you want... I enjoyed it, not everyone will. Don't go in thinking you'll be treated to mind-blowing sci-fi, action of Matrix proportions or execution, or something that will make you re-think your life... instead, just know that the action is awesome more often than it isn't, and that not-rid-of-clichés plot is not as stupid as that of an awful lot of sci-fi action fare. I recommend this to those interested in what I describe immediately preceding this sentence. Fans of the show may find themselves disappointed. 6/10

reviews.review_text: Aeon Flux is a mess but it's a fascinating and intriguing mess. Aeon Flux is a science fiction adventure film that includes a lot of intriguing ideas, some of which are left underdeveloped. The script, credited to Phil Hay & Matt Mandredi (based on Peter Chung's MTV animated shorts), doesn't seem to know whether it wants to be smart enough to appeal to serious-minded movie-goers or dumb enough to appeal to popcorn-munchers. So it vacillates and, ultimately, that becomes its undoing. However, except during a few routine action sequences that fail to raise a single nape hair, Aeon Flux is never uninteresting.Early in the film, there's a nice action scene featuring pods that spit darts and grass that might cut the lawn mower (rather than the other way around). After that, the "exciting" stuff becomes routine: running around, blowing things up, shooting, etc. The ideas underlying Aeon Flux's plot are the film's strength, and the filmmakers deserve some credit for doing more than paying lip service to them.

reviews.review_text: I guess it's more fun making some movies than watching them. You get to go on location, eat and drink at the producer's expense, have a great time. All this thing did was bore us.Well, they had their fun at our expense. Will there be a consequence? Doesn't seem like it. They'll just go ahead and make another "art film" and the reviewers will hype it to death, and we'll go see it and complain again. Why? Because we're stupid? No, because we have more faith in the goodness of human nature than these con artists have.

A fine acting job by the actors/actresses were ruined by the s-l-o-w pace of the movie. It took forever for things to happen. At many points in the movie you are just watching Bill Murray gaze off into space for what seems like eternity. No dialogue, no movement. Just nothing. I know this happens in real life, but in 105 minute movie; 20-30 minutes shouldn't be spent on absolutely nothing. Bill Murray, playing his role brilliantly, adds to this slow paced feeling. He speaks very little, letting his expressions do his talking and when he does talk he shows no affect. The one person who added a little life to the movie was Jeffrey Wright, who turned in a credible role as the friend/neighbor. The bottom line is don't see the movie if you are tired. The pacing may put you to right to sleep.

Obviously the director was more interested in having Murray show how empty his life was at 50. Unfortunately, without some kind of back story, I found it really hard to believe he had Sharon Stone, Jessica Lange, and Tilda Swinton hot for him in a 5-6 month period when he was 30. I expected to see some spark of something that made him attractive to these fabulous women (he wasn't rich at 30), but I didn't see it. What exactly did Delpy and Lolita girl (and even the flower girl at the cemetery) see in him at 50? I first thought maybe the references to Don Juan and Don Johnson were supposed to gentle put downs against a guy that obviously did not fit the bill. But every character did think Murray was quite the stud with a big rep. Maybe that's the look for 2005: a balding, graying slug in a polyester sweat suit.

I love Jarmusch's style - there are very few directors today who approach film-making in such a unique way (maybe Todd Solondz). This movie was incredible. I like Murray and he excels in his role as a retired computer businessman? who is well-retired and believes he has a son from a lover 20 years earlier. If you have a Short-Attention-Span than this movie and Jarmusch are not for you. The pacing fits the character development and the silence-as-script approach that is pure Jarmusch. As he visits each of his lovers in turn to surreptitiously detect his sons' mother (and the writer of the letter that starts his quest), he encounters women who are the same as he remembers and at the same time very different. His journey raises more questions about all concerned than it answers and he does not know which way to turn, so he turns in all directions. I highly recommend this and hope it gets a wider distribution.

Eccentric and episodic filmmaker Jim Jarmusch ("Dead Man," "Mystery Train," "Down By Law") teams up with the master of the deadpan, Bill Murray ("The Life Aquatic"), for one of the most thoughtful and meaningful movies of the year. As his current girlfriend, Sherry (Julia Delpy, "Before Sunset") is leaving him, confirmed bachelor, Don Johnston (Murray), receives a pink letter informing him that he has a son approaching 20 years of age. Shocked by this revelation, he tells wacky Ethiopian neighbor, Winston (Jeffrey Wright, "Ali," "The Manchurian Candidate"), who plans an entire travel itinerary for Johnston to seek out past lovers and try find his son. Winston, who loves detective novels, goes about solving the mystery like a budget Sherlock Homes, examining and re-examining the pink envelope and its contents for any clue whatsoever. Johnston wants no part of this, however, believing the entire thing is a joke. Still, he takes the trip, not only discovering what several past girlfriends (Sharon Stone, Francis Conroy, Jesseca Lange and Tilda Swinton) are doing now, but just how shallow and manliness's his Don Juan lifestyle has been. The film is sort of like "Sideways" for the manically-depressed, and Jarmusch's quirky style and long pauses may take some getting used to, but it's well worth the time. There are also some classic comedy moments, such as when Stone's teenage nymphet of a daughter (appropriately named "Lolita") puts the moves on him; and when he is forced to have a really uptight dinner with real estate agent Conroy and her uptight husband (Christopher McDonald, "Happy Gilmore"). Murray doesn't run the gamut of emotions he did in his Oscar-nominated turn in "Lost In Translation," but he can communicate a feeling with a smirk or frown better than most actors today can with five pages of dialogue. It's an excellent performance. On the other side of the acting coin is Wright, who soars with enthusiasm for Johnston's journey, planning everything down to the letter. It's fun and he balances Murray perfectly. despite the fine acting all around, one of my favorite aspects of the film was the terrific original African jazz soundtrack by Mulate Astatke, which was as much a part of the motion picture as the dialogue.

reviews.review_text: Went into D.C. on Saturday to see Broken Flowers at the Landmark Theatre there. It was such an excellent movie. Bill Murray played his role of Don Johnston flawlessly. Sharon Stone was pretty damn good for the short time she was in the film. And they both actually played off of each other pretty well.The movie was totally a Jim Jarmusch movie though. I think a lot of people were worried that he was going "mainstream" with this movie. But all worries are put to rest after seeing the movie, it is a Jarmusch film all the way. Everything about it screams Jim Jarmusch; the story, characters, humor, cinematography, editing, music, and pacing are all Jarmusch. I love it.I am sure some people who see it, might find the pacing a bit slow. As my girlfriend put it, "It's paced like a french film." But that is high praise coming from her. All of Jarmusch's films are paced a bit slow though. They aren't about the big events in life that most movies center around. They are usually about the small things, that most of us don't even bother thinking about. I think that gives his movies a bit more realism than most movies though. And that is part of these reason I love his films.Spoilers Below - This movie is also much more about the journey than it is about the destination. I love how the ending is left very open to interpretation. The one kid he met could be his son, but probably not. Or his son could still be out there somewhere, anywhere. He could be any kid that Don sees on the street. Or he may not have a son at all, the letter could be a Hoax, done by a couple different people.The evidence is put forth for a couple theories, but a definite answer is never given. We never know for sure. But it also doesn't matter, the movie isn't about who or where his son is. It is about him looking back at his life, and seeing what was, what could have been, and what is. Such an awesome movie.

Films this restrained can only be made by an experienced filmmaker, a guy who knows what he wants to say and how to say it and doesn't have to worry about impressing everyone with witty banter or fancy camera tricks. Broken Flowers is so restrained, I'm sure it will elicit some of the same responses Bill Murray's last two films (The Life Aquatic, Lost in Translation) received, mainly  what's the big fuss about? The big fuss is that like Jim Jarmusch, Murray's an experienced craftsman, who understands that true talent lies in how much you give to your supporting actors, not in how much spotlight you take. Movie acting is all in the eyes and subtle body language, not in bombast. but mostly it's in being able to listen to your fellow actors. It's counterintuitive, that a visual medium relies so much on quiet, but it's what separates the great performances from the over-hyped. Let's hope that a subtle movie like this one avoids massive media attention, as that would be missing its point. And what, many may ask, is the point of Broken Flowers. At the screening I attended many were confused, others disappointed by the ending. Indeed, if there is one niggling detail that separates this film from perfection, it is the ending. Of course, Indian rugmakers intentionally weave mistakes into their wares, because they believe only God is perfect, my point being that the theme of this film is that in a quest for meaning, sometimes we learn there is no answer or that the answer is complex. In this case, Jarmusch seems to be saying that meaning is already present, but you might only glean it if you are prepared. Murray's character, Don Johnston (with a "T"), only went on the road trip at his neighbour's urging, and clearly felt the whole thing was nonsense. His attitude may have caused him to miss the mystery, but discover new truths. Similarly, the audience may become too fixated with solving the mystery of who the mother of his son is and miss the other truths, namely that Johnston already has a family with his next-door neighbours, and he already has a relationship as good as he would have had with any of his past flames. The pink typewritten letter, the long-lost son, they are not the point of his life. As Johnston himself says, "The past is gone, the future's not here yet. All there is is now."

reviews.review_text: I was lucky enough to get a sneak preview through the Traverse City Film Festival last night. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed it. "Broken Flowers," I guess, is supposed to be this long, contemplative film about a man's journey into his past to discover how his life and history of loves has added up. Initially, the film is structured as a mystery - as Bill Murray's character tries to find the old girlfriend who bore his son, but it's more about the journey than the destination.But, to me, this movie was one of the most boring things I've ever sat through. There are an endless number of minutes-long takes of Bill Murray driving a car by himself. There are several scenes of him sitting alone in his living room, listening to the stereo and thinking. A couple of these scenes, where the silences could be meaningful and carry depth, would be fine in a film like this, if the film carried more weight or gave Murray's character more of a background than "a bemused, aging Don Juan." Instead, once the movie ends, I felt like it contained several good scenes where Murray interacted with the old girlfriends and about 30 minutes of dead air. Why, why, WHY were there four editing cuts done as Murray drove a Taurus down a country road? Wouldn't one shot establish the plot point as much as is necessary? I get it. He's driving.Oh, and I figured out that Murray's character was an aging Don Juan within the first five minutes, when he's watching the movie about Don Juan. I didn't need to have Julie Delpy call him "Don Juan," then have Jeffrey Wright call him "Don Juan," then have everyone comment on how his name is Don Johnston. I get the point. Don't hammer it into the ground.This is not a good movie. If it gets across-the-board good reviews, I'll be baffled. It's pretentious, meaningless and doesn't go very far. It doesn't function as a mystery. It doesn't function successfully as an illustration of a character. Good actors, like Jessica Lange, Frances Conroy and Sharon Stone, are given little to do in episodic scenes.All in all, the emperor's not wearing any clothes.

There has been a lot of talk that "Broken Flowers" is Jim Jarmusch's most commercially accessible film to date. One can almost hear Jarmusch muttering something reactionary like "commercial? That's just a label." It's a label that some Jarmusch fans might associate with "selling out". But selling out does not apply to Jim Jarmusch. He still has complete control of his work and is still the only American filmmaker who owns his own negatives. If "Broken Flowers" does break into the mainstream, it is nothing overly deliberate. Jarmusch makes familiar films that seem intimate in their tone. He toys with old themes while still leaving his films open to interpretation. "Broken Flowers" is a travelogue and like most Jarmusch films, the story is more concerned with the journey but not so much about the destination. Bill Murray plays Don Johnston, a man who we know little about. We know he's single and we know he's had some flame's in the past. The last one just walked out on him. When Don receives an anonymous letter from one of these old flames, he learns that he has a twenty year old son who might be looking for him." Don thinks this is a joke but takes the advice from a friend to unfold the mystery by tracking down his past flings. He flies somewhere to a generic American place, rents a car and begins his investigation. Each ex has an individual personality but most of them share something similar. They are content and have moved on from the past. One of the ex's we meet works in real estate and decides it would be a good idea for her to get into the water business because "one day in the near future it will be more valuable then oil." The atmosphere is awkward and rather then care whether this woman is responsible for the anonymous letter, we just feel like getting out of there. The film's journey is absurd in many ways because we are never sure what the real point is. What is Don going to do if he does find his son? This where Bill Murray's credit as an actor shines through. We see from his small facial gestures that he is empty, and sad. There is a sense of longing as if life took a wrong turn somewhere and it is only now that he is realizing it. The ending of "Broken Flowers" is what really makes the film special. Don't expect too much or too little. Just see it. Its inspiring, hopeful and better then any other movie this year. The film also has a great soundtrack by Ethiopian musician, Mulatu Astatke. And we see in the credits that Jarmusch dedicated the film to French filmmaker Jean Eustache. Jean Eustache made a phenomenal film in the 1960's titled, "The Mother and The Whore". He had an influence on John Cassavetes and likewise both had an influence on Jim Jarmusch.

reviews.review_text: Bill Murray changed his facial expression only once that I can remember during the entire movie. He moves like a robot. Like Lost in Translation, his character moves from scene to scene, place to place, apparently only because his friend Winston tells him to, and then he comes home, gets back in his jogging suit and goes back to his apparently pointless life. It is not ever clear, and possibly only barely suggested, that anything at all is changing in his mind or his heart. I take that back. Heart is barely suggested. He seems like someone who has been injected with Novocaine throughout his body. An extremely boring movie.

This is the kind of movie critics love, film majors swoon over, and the rest of us can't get too excited about.I see it as an exercise in minimalism. Given a talented star and supporting cast, a known director, cool soundtrack music, and a green light from the studio, can you make a successful movie with a minimalist script? A script that doesn't contain much? That gives the star precious few lines and instructs him to show as little emotion as possible? That gives the next-door neighbor a much more interesting character? After seeing it, I'm thinking, well, it's different, it's OK, but I don't consider it a great movie, or a successful movie, or even one I'll want to see again. I don't recommend that you go out and pay $9.00 to see it.

reviews.review_text: I'm more of fan of Jim Jarmusch than Bill Murray, but I think his performance in Broken Flowers is the highlight of the movie. His ubiquitous deadpan never carried so much weight as in this role as the aging Don Juan character, Don Johnston. A strong rebuff to those that thought Lost in Translation was his one-of-a-kind-role-of-a-lifetime etc. Broken Flowers is a Jim Jarmusch film that belongs with the best of his work (Down By Law, Mystery Train, Dead Man, Ghost Dog) - films that entertain and provoke thought in equal measure, that keep the sense of auteur vision without sacrificing accessibility. I was disappointed by Coffee and Cigarettes, but this film restored my faith in Mr. Jarmusch. It's especially good to see him using a format which retains elements of anthology but stays together as a single story, albeit one which ultimately chooses character study over a perfectly sewn-up plot. Some viewers may be frustrated by the inconclusiveness of the ending. I don't think the film could end any other way and remain true to the character, the tone, or the vision. It's a little downbeat from start to finish, and you either buy it or you don't. I bought it. Jeffrey Wright was very funny and warm, Sharon Stone plays trailer trash perfectly, fine cameos by Jessica Lange (as an 'animal communicator'), Julie Delpy, Chloe Sevigny, and Tilda Swinton (cast against type as a biker chick.) Plus Alexis Dziena as the Lolita to end all Lolitas, whom I would gladly see more of (in a manner of speaking).

reviews.review_text: Spare me. This movie is well directed and well paced. The inner core of a man's soul, a man's feelings, and what it will take for that man to reach these. But this movie, with all it's awkward silences, awkward moments and awkward characters........just leads you to an awkward ending. So the man can feel again, so the man thinks every young man is his son now. So what ? I was subdued for the ride in this movie. I loved the scene where he is standing outside his motel room in the early morning......listening and watching the world go by around him. Busy.......but peaceful. The director reaches the audience in so many ways with this film, but then falls flat on his face with an ending that is one of those "thought provoking" or " making his point". Just shut up already. End the movie with just that. An ending!! You develop likable and intriguing characters, don't utilize them, and then end it with hokey pokey.Come on Bill, great acting, great story.........but no direction. Slap the director next time and tell him to have some backbone and finish his movie the right way.

Am I the only one who judges a movie by how I feel when I leave the theater. The movie itself might be imperfect, might have a few sections that drag on a tad, or are cut a bit short, but all in all the sharp reflections on life color my own life when I leave the theater and stop and get an ice cream; blueberry swirl on a regular cone perhaps, maybe some jimmies.We meet Don, Winston and his family and the women Don has "known" (real estate saleswoman, animal communicator, closet reorganizer and biker chick in sticks)and mentally dissect the patterns in which their individual lives are constructed. It makes one think of their own life (me at least) and how we have a choice in the direction our lives are going and how it can lead to happiness, unhappiness or ennui. (Some people might disagree with me and think the couple who sell real estate in the Mcmansion are happy, but they would be a little fruity now wouldn't they.) And then we meet the hungry young man in front of the diner, with his sad angry eyes and gruff manner, and I really want to get to know the guy, where he's been, what's he's been through. We don't get to, and neither does Don, and I think that is sort of the point.It was great to see Don come alive at the end, running after the kid that might be his son. Even if he didn't get himself an instant Mcfamily on his road trip, at least he achieved a desire to rethink the patterns in his life, and direction he is going in.All in all a great film, a nice walk home, and some great ice cream:)

reviews.review_text: BROKEN FLOWERS (2005) **** Bill Murray, Jeffrey Wright, Sharon Stone, Frances Conroy, Jessica Lange, Tilda Swinton, Julie Delpy, Alexis Dziena, Chloe Sevigny, Mark Webber, Chris Bauer, Christopher McDonald, Pell James, Heather Simms, Jennifer Rapp. (Dir: James Jarmusch). Bill Murray continues his blue period of middle-age angst and anomie after his trifecta of subtle, low-key hangdog dudes in Wes Anderson's "Rushmore", Sofia Coppola's "Lost in Translation" and Anderson's "The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou" (and an asterisk for Anderson's "The Royal Tennebaum"'s as well) but never before has he seemed so melancholic contemplative about staring into the abyss with the abyss staring right back at him then in filmmaker Jim Jarmusch's comic valentine of man-o-pause with bittersweet revelations and life lessons.Murray stars as the glum computer magnate Don Johnston (yes a variation on the iconic monikers Don Juan and sex symbol Don Johnson, both ladies' men with charm to spare) who - in the process of his latest flame Sherry (a pouty Delpy) leaving him to his dimly lit modest split level house in the tony Hudson Valley, NY area – receives a mysterious letter in red ink on pink stationery informing him that he has a 19 year old son and that the writer, one of his old paramours, neglects to provide a key clue: a signature.Prompting curiosity he won't admit to, Don goes next door to apparently his only friend, Winston (the genius Wright mixing a fine comic blend to the dry tonic of Murray), a happily married, three job wielding family man with a lovely brood of several young children and doting wife who take to Don as a de-facto uncle, - his polar opposite, who upon reading the mash note of fidelity decides to delve into finding out who in fact sent the letter. Winston is a wanna-be mystery writer and this quenches his creative juices by setting a course of action for a very reluctant Don to journey into his past , a place he seriously doesn't want to reflect upon. After Don jots down a list of past lovers and Winston does some mean Googling – discovering one sadly has passed away – find four possible suspects. With the aid of MapQuest Winston has booked Don on a flight and rented a car for him to pursue the knowledge that will lead him to some satisfaction, whether he likes it or not.What follows is a decidedly uneven-keeled trek into despair, lost love and finally acceptance as Don meets up with Laura (a remarkably good Stone), a solemn yet flaky beauty who organizes closet space, who has a provocatively named daughter Lolita (comely Dziena) providing some comic ribbing from her literarily given moniker (and defining it as well with some eye-opening and jaw-dropping moments of casual undressing); Dora (Conroy providing some substantial loss of things past with a sad dignity), a former flower child cum realtor married to her partner in business and jerk husband (McDonald in perfect SOB form as he's accustomed); Carmen (an earthily slightly bitter Lange), an animal 'communicator' whose very personal assistant (an icy Sevigny) barely holds back her contempt for the unannounced comings of Don; and finally Penny (Swinton getting in touch with her inner Cate Blanchett), whose anger is not even close to contained when Don encounters her briefly with a sudden tinge of violence brimming at the surface throughout the odyssey.Jarmusch lets his leisurely paced tale take its root in the simple premise of a somewhat successful and selfish man come to terms with his mortality and the realness of his existence: a hollow shell of what he possibly was (or could've been) with some sharp nuances in his economic script allowing his dream cast several wonderful moments to get their chops around. The female ensemble combined would be the perfect woman and that just may be one of the messages attempting to form in Don's psyche as he discovers many things he never understood about his past relationships. One note of trivia, the final sequence cameos Murray's real-life son Homer. But it is hands down Murray's finest, most subtle work that anchors his melancholia with a twist of sardonic after-thoughts seeping thru as he wanders the roads to his hopeful ultimate reward: knowing himself. The red herring of his parenthood not withstanding the conceit works in self-discovery no matter how painful it can be. (Don's last sojourn to the one girlfriend's grave is smartly shown with some genuine grief). Murray does so much by using so little of his facial muscles to register how he acts and reacts (at one point when Winston has enlisted him in this fateful trip he says something to the fact that Don must know what women want and there is a shadow of revulsion at that happy thought that cascades ever so lightly across his face) and for me the singular moment that truly captures the mood of the film is on the eve of his descent as he sits solo in his home quietly listening to the pangs of Marvin Gaye's soulful "I Want You" brought tears to my eyes and a rock in my throat. And this is before the madness that will ensue! You just want to give him a hug and a noogie and say, "Getoutta here, everything's going to be alright".I truly hope the Academy has the balls again to nominate not only Murray for one of his best performances but actually give the poor bastard a golden boy this year and for Jarmusch if not for his skillfully off-center direction then for his original screenplay. The duo teamed up briefly a year ago in the seemingly improvised "Coffee and Cigarettes" and Jarmusch wrote this solely with Murray in mind. Both should be proud of themselves for doing the impossible: making a jerk into a mensch.

reviews.review_text: After viewing the trailer, I was hopeful that Broken Flowers might prove to be a subtly humorous and sweet film such as Lost in Translation, which I very much liked. But by the end I, and my family, couldn't believe we had been made to sit through two hours of excruciatingly slow pacing for no seeming reason.I am not a film buff, but am a theater person. Though I don't know all of Jarmusch's previous films, tactics, or techniques, I do understand some basic principles of storytelling, and I feel that this did not meet them satisfactorily. It is a beautiful and satisfying thing for the writer to leave something to the audiences' imagination, making them engage their imaginations to complete the story rather than remain passive viewers who are spoon fed answers and entertainment.But this can be taken too far, and I felt that the film left too much to the audience, without providing enough meat to sink our imaginations into.The one really touching moment came,I thought, when at the end of his list of former girlfriends, he visits a graveyard and the gravestone of a former flame. A close shot catches Murray with tears welling in his eyes. This would have been a terrific moment...if we hadn't been made to wait so long that we didn't even care.I agree with other comments that I saw little to no trace of the Don Juan that could have attracted so many women (including the four women in the film whom he supposedly bedded the same year). Even if he had had an incredible vigor in the past, why would he have a gorgeous girlfriend apparently 20 years his junior at present? And what does he want? I was never able to discover that. Without any seeming motivation and without the development of relationships or any type of build that culminated in anything significant, I felt cheated by the end. Any point that could be made in the film feels like it could have been made in the first 30 minutes. After that it was just more of the same. Whereas Lost in Translation made a statement about the loneliness of two people in a foreign country by its slow pace, it also interwove the pacing with a touching and unconventional relationship that gave the audience something to engage in and watch develop. Nothing seemed to develop here. Which raises the question, Why should we care?

reviews.review_text: Fans of Dame Daphne Du Maurier will appreciate the gently moving plot of this film... and the ending that doesn't quite give you closure. The guy sitting in the row behind us commented with frustration at the end: "Gee, that was a great film. Where's the rest of it???" Well, the clues are everywhere, if you look for them. The title, which I liked, is the thread running through this movie.(I did want to smack Bill Murray's character a couple of times to speed him up a bit...)Definitely see this film. The photography and music alone make it worthwhile. Bill Murray is subtle, cool, sad, and funny all at the same time. The story is both a mystery and an adventure. And of course there's the fun of guessing the locations of his travels. Pay attention and use your imagination.

reviews.review_text: I don't know when I've watched a film that bored me more than this one. Nothing EVER happens. And in the end, nothing is resolved. The only sparks of life are Tilda Swinton's white trash character (though she only gets about 1 minute of screen time), and a briefly naked teenager (too obviously named "Lolita").The misguided applause Bill Murray received for "Lost in Translation" has obviously convinced him (and his director) that kudos is to be found in the concealed musings of an apathetic, deadpan character; one that we can neither love nor bother hating. Until I have some proof that he has returned to his earlier ("Groundhog Day") form, or at least that he is breathing, I won't be seeing any more Bill Murray pictures.And this film is a SHOCKING waste of Swinton, Jeffrey Wright, Frances Conroy, Sharon Stone, Jessica Lange and Julie Delpy.

This is the unsuccessful sequel to Lost in Translation that shows no understanding of what made the original work. It is an hour and forty-five minutes of Bill Murray making faces, pretty scenery going to and from airports, a series of ambiguous clues and a mystery that is resolved only by the credits rolling. The dialog is calculated, the humor is either overly broad and flat or simply flat, with punchlines than never arrive. This movie has the muted tones of an art film, but there is little art. There are only the same ingredients, thrown together with a prayer, but it is a prayer that is not answered. Rarely have I felt so mislead by popular critics.
