reviews.review_text: It's a bit of an ordeal to read through the user comments on Land of the Dead - they range from every extreme to every other; some say there's too much of this or that, while others claim there's too little of the same things. Oh well.Anyway, I am not a particular fan of zombies or horror, but I am a fan of social commentary, and that's what's interesting about Romero's zombie movies. The high point, as most people agree, was 1978's Dawn of the Dead, in which the zombies symbolized mindless consumers. Since then, not much has changed in society on this account, except that people have become even less aware of social problems - a good example was the 2004 Dawn of the Dead remake, which was sadly cleansed of any social commentary whatsoever.Land of the Dead sees Romero return to the social commentary, and commendably it's quite radical. Here, the zombies have taken on a new symbolism; now they represent the poor masses, the alienated working classes, who, fed up with being reduced to an inhuman existence, finally develop a sense of compassion and solidarity for their fellow zombie (i.e., on the non-literal level, human being), and revolts, bringing down decadent capitalism. This is great.I have no problem with the movie not being in proper continuity with the previous movies; this one is its own story, and should be regarded independently.Gorewise, I was neither impressed nor repulsed. It wasn't terribly grisly, and the horror effects didn't really affect me (but then, they rarely do).Unfortunately, the story is not fully rounded. If the zombies are the good guys, then what about the (good? Neutral?) human characters? What do they signify? And if I have a main complaint about the movie, it's probably Asia Argento's part. That girl is the coolest thing on the northern hemisphere, and here she had hardly anything to do, nor was her character explored at all. There must have been a reason for her being thrown into the zombie cage in the first place, but this is not explained. I was also disappointed that there was no romantic or sexual interaction between her and the main guy. All they managed was to exchange bedroom eyes at the end. Not so much as a kiss did we see. Drat!Still, Land of the Dead was a successful movie in terms of symbolical content. All in all, pretty good. Not on par with Dawn of the Dead, of course, but in my opinion probably the second-best of Romero's zombie movies.8 out of 10.

That movie was great...I know you people were expecting gore, blah, blah , blah! But hello!!! we live in 2005!! there is something called the FCC!!! He wasn't going to get away with a whole lot, but he did get away with a lot of excellent FX, more than what I was expecting. He sure did get in his political side because there are a lot of references to how much a dick George Bush is!S get off your ass and see that Romero made another excellent flick!!! reviews.review_text: I am a huge horror movie fan and I would like to say that i thought it was probably the worst movie that i have ever seen. I am a huge fan of the original Night of the Living Dead so I expected something great out of Romero. By the end of the movie, it felt almost painful to watch. The plot was lacking, and nothing really happened during the entire movie. You can only watch someones arm being chewed on so much, and buildings being blown up. There was no explanation as to why the Zombies rose from the dead, or how they being "smart and were able to communicate". In 28 Days Later, they took the classic Zombie movie and gave it a plot.. Which made it one of the best Zombie movies i have seen in a long time. Romeros movie focused solely on gore and little else. Leaving the movie, i was upset that i had wasted an hour and a half of my life. Stay at home and don't waste your money.

'Land of the Dead' is a welcome return to the 'traditional' zombie genre perfected by George Romero in his Dead trilogy (now a quadrilogy). The original 'Dawn of the Dead' was a wonderful mixture of social satire and gut-wrenching horror but Romero got away from that for the most part in 'Day of the Dead'. Except for the re-training of Bud, 'Day' was just a gore-splashed finale to what had been a terrific series. But 'Land' takes this whole thing in a new direction, mixing in the social satire with excessive gore and an interesting and oddly sad conclusion (only George Romero could turn a zombie into a sympathetic creature). It was scary (and not just in those 'jump-out-at-you' scenes) and it was gory (Romero found new ways to have zombies attack and devour people) and it was fun. I like how the city took on the traditional look of the old medieval castle - with the upper caste living in luxury inside the inner wall and the poor living in squalor inside the outer wall. And the fact that these zombies are beginning to think brings up something I had wondered about during 'Dawn of the Dead' - namely, if radiation had reactivated their brains, why wouldn't some activity be reactivated in the cerebral cortex as well? I liked the remake of 'Dawn of the Dead,' but 'Land of the Dead' was a better movie.

reviews.review_text: I loved the movie but i had some problems with aspects of it. I like to whine so bear with me.CONTAINS SPOILERS The scene at the fence is not believable. In the first place, you could simply throw a piece of debris over the fence and walk over it. You could shove someone into it and walk over them. You could shove a zombie into it and climb over it. In any case, once the zombies advanced, at least one or more of the people would have fallen backwards into the fence. I am sure that a few people would have chosen to try to jump the fence and die rather than get chewed up.There is no possibility of a financial system like the one shown occurring. Money would be worthless as you could go to a bank and pick up a few thousand. Also, this situation would arise: A poor person would go outside, grab food, bring it back, sell it, and use the money to buy some of the food he just grabbed. That doesn't make any sense.There were three deaths that could have been easily avoided in the movie by using some common, low tech materials. A human, dead or alive, can't bite very hard because of the structure of the jaw. Police officers have access to gloves and outfits that can withstand attacks by packs of dogs. Divers have shark resistant gloves and body suits. Atheletes have hardened body armor, helmets, and other devices that would prevent bites. Why was no one wearing these low tech, common devices?I came back to lower my score from a 9 to a 5 because i saw it on DVD. Here are some things i noticed:1) An able person cannot physically pull the arm off of another person. You can't do it. A zombie with little physical strength could not pull an arm off of a person. 2) In the scene where the soldier in the jeep gets bitten by the nearly headless zombie, someone seems to have missed the fact that you need the muscles in your neck to bite. Without a neck there is no possibility of "being chewed".

I've been waiting years for this film, or so it feels, and I was not disappointed. Romero has brought back to a world where the dead now outnumber the living and the survivors are hold up in what they think is an impregnable city. The film also continues the trend started in Day of the Dead, and the zombies are beginning to evolve and learn. This was the one aspect of the film that I feared would not work, but it fits in perfectly into his world.Romero is even more on form than I could have possibly hoped. The effects, the story, and the pacing of the movie were spot on. If you love horror, zombies, or gore up the wall, then this is the film for you. If you are a fan of Romero's earlier films then prepare to be blown away.The master has returned. 10/10.

reviews.review_text: I was very...very...VERY disappointed with this movie. I had so high expectations with this movie after "Dawn Of The Dead" (2005) that this...for me is pure trash.-The movie immediately starts with a developed after-infected world, zombies and humans are living in the same region but separated, and the humans live in some sort of mall like nothing is going on instead of moving somewhere else???...hello?!?!?! -Zombies ARE NOT SUPPOSED TO HAVE INTELLIGENCE!!!, in this movie the zombies DO have intelligence and that really takes them off their characteristic.-Now, in previous zombie movies the word "zombie" is never said, in this movie it is said like 30 times!!! -The gore effects are way way WAY too much and way too surreal, way too much blood.-Ok, now, the "leader zombie" drives me crazy 'cause he looks so dumb!!! I mean, when he angrily screams looks stupid, when he tries to figure out how to use the gun looks stupid...-The ending is so stupid!!! It kinda makes you feel like everything is over even when the zombies are still alive.-And, above all, what was the plot of the movie??? The zombies suddenly trying to get to the humans???...out of nowhere???-Oh, and just so you know, the movie IS NOT SCARY!!!The movie is NO WHERE NEAR GOOD, is one of those movies you see once and you don't want to see again. I don't to who recommend this film, I guess to Romero's fans.

I am a Romero fan, but not to the extent where I am blind. The Romero films I have seen post-Day of the Dead are missing something that made his earlier films unique and special. Dark Half is terrible. Monkey Shines is fairly enjoyable but is like a Channel5 movie (you'll understand if you're from the UK). LOTD is much better than those two, but still without character. While no-one can deny they cared about Roger, Peter, Stephen & Fran in Dawn of the Dead, I found little empathy with any characters in Land. There was some interesting gore scenes, but when Tom Savini is so good at his job, why use CGI?I still find Day to be the goriest zombie flick ever, and why do they save Director's Cut for DVD's? It should be the other way around. Dawn is and always will be the best. It's the most entertaining zombie flick made. It has great characters and great ideas, and it's a lot of fun. Day is a much more serious film, and while not as good, it is very sinister and scary. Land almost seems to be trying to capture elements of both, but it doesn't work. It's neither unsettling or scary, nor funny or well scripted.First and foremost this movie was too short. For such an apocalyptic tale 93 minutes is a bit hasty. There never seemed to be any sense of foreboding throughout the film. The zombies were there, but there was never any real fear they would take over. It seemed obvious that they would be defeated. The fate of Hopper was all too plain to see and was not near as interesting as the deaths of the bikers in Dawn or Capt. Rhodes in Day (Possibly one of the best death scenes ever).The diminutive time scale of the movie affected the story also, as the only zombie that managed to learn  Big Daddy (all the rest just followed) learned far too quickly for my liking. It's like the zombies had obviously been around for a very long time, but then Big Daddy decides to suddenly start to learn in these 93 minutes? I prefer the idea of zombies learning en masse, like what was suggested in the original DOTD when it is discovered the zombies are able to use things as basic tools or weapons, or learning at a slower pace, like Bub in DOTD. I just found it a bit hard to accept this one intelligent zombie out of the millions(?). Although the rest of the zombies following the leader is more 'acceptable' and also keeping in-line with Stephen in Dawn & Bub in Day. The premise of the movie was essentially good (the zombies realising they are under attack from 'norms' and retaliating), it just happened too fast. Perhaps Romero would have been better off plagiarising himself and having a zombie who used to live in the city and wants to get back (much like Stephen in Dawn).I didn't like Hopper as Kaufman, he just isn't scary enough. I didn't hate him as much as I should have and so I wasn't looking forward to his death as much as I would have liked, I also found it unlikely he would be in such a position what with his rather cowardly attitude. Kris Kristofferson would have been a wiser choice (I recently saw him in Silver City  he can be very scary!)I also felt this film was a bit too self-aware and Romero seemed to be deliberately making 'social commentaries', evidently because of so many people discussing what is being said, and what is really being said, in Dawn.Something is missing that I can't explain. In Dawn (and Day to some extent) I love the lads taking pot shots at the zombies, running them over, killing as many as possible. In Land (and the Dawn remake) I didn't find it so exciting. Maybe it's something to do with the original Dawn seeming like fun whereas the others seem more serious. I dunno.Despite this, Land was not un-entertaining and the 93 minutes flew by. Asia Argento was pretty good, Simon Baker was OK if slightly two dimensional, John Leguizamo has an annoying lopsided mouth and reminds me of a young Williem DaFoe. No one else has much of a part in it. The ending left a few loose ends  considering the world was meant to be taken over, and out of all the zombies that were lined up on the pier  there wasn't many to blow up at the end. Any regular army could have taken them out. And they also seem to have forgotten about all the zombies that were actually still inside the Kaufman's complex.

reviews.review_text: Romeros latest zombie epic is an entertaining bit of post apocalyptic horror.While its no way as good as dawn of the dead, its vast improvement over the piece of crap that was day of the dead.While this time round the zombies have evolved and have gotten smarter(they play trumpets and everything !)the real shocking revelation is what the world has turned into. The rich live in a shielded metropolis and live on goods taken from the zombie infested outside world by the poor who live in broken down ghettos.The films depiction of a post zombie struck world is very well handled.Performance wise, its john liguazamo and dennis hopper (who haven't battled each other on screen since super mario bros)who shine here with liguazamo as disgruntled zombie buster cholo and dennis hopper as a villainous president (who said this film wasn't realistic?).The zombies them selves (who are now smarter) look more nasty and realistic than ever before and the zombie attack sequences and gore ,like the other movies before it, are creepy and well orchestrated.The finale is no way as tense as dawn and the ending is a little vague but land of the dead is a good (if not spectacular) addition to Romero's DEAD series.

reviews.review_text: If you don't expect too much from the script or the acting you will do fine with the real premise of this movie which is to kill lots of people in really creative and gory ways. On that note, this movie delivers full force! This is one of the better zombie movies but not as good as Dawn of The Dead 2004. Dennis Hopper's presence is a liability as has been common with his recent attempts at "acting". The casting is pathetic in it's blind swing at being politically correct and including as many races as possible and even a Jar-Jar Banks style sidekick to the hero of this movie in the form of a retarded burn victim who is a sharpshooter in between really lame jokes and clumsy attempts at acting his role. The characters are two dimensional and the plot is one dimensional, but we came to see some mutha's get their intestines ripped out of their stomach and then lit on fire while they get shot with hundreds of rounds of armor piercing bullets. That is what this movie offers, unfortunately and sadly- there is nothing else in the way of realism, atmosphere or character development to hold it all together. As an interesting movie, it fails miserably- as a vehicle for mass graphic slaughter- it does quite nicely! Lots of blood and intestines being gobbled and heads chopped off. So be in the right mood for this when you watch it.Also be prepared for poor cinematography- this looks like a movie set in every scene with what I call 80's lighting and the 80's cleanliness factor- meaning characters that should be dirty are all spiffy wearing clean costumes and looking very fake as a result. I was surprised to see someone in 2005 use this absolute crap el cheapo lame-o method of cinematography and obviously fake 80's dramatic lighting still. I also hated the character of the zombie leader he was just stupid and a very poor casting choice. His big line was "unhhhh!".Same genre and BETTER than this by far: Dawn of The Dead 2004, 28 Days Later 2002. What made these movies better by far is the cinematography and the scripts- they actually had those elements.This movie delivers on gore factor but falls flat on it's face with the script, the characters and acting and the cinematography. I give this a 4 instead of a 5 because of the Jar-Jar Banks-like sidekick burn victim sidekick/comedic relief plot device- he's very annoying.

This movie starts off as the usual zombie trash. Zombies have somehow taken over the world and there is one city that has electric fences around it to try and keep them out. A novel twist was put in to try and make news to the old gore fest and screams which are all in Romero's horror movies. The zombies are getting smart and using guns. This film fails to do what the others all fail to do which is answer this question: WHY DO ZOMBIES WANT TO EAT PEOPLE? Will someone please explain this to me. If they are dead, how do they get energy from food and how does their brain still function? A zombie bites a man on the hand and the man turns into a zombie without first dying. This implies that it is some sort of infection which turns people into zombies. BUT when a man died without being bitten, he became a zombie as well without being infected. A zombie fired a gun instead of eating a human and taught the others to do the same. Was their insatiable appetite suddenly satisfied after being taught by the leader. The plot is so predictable. In every single one of Romero's zombie films, the zombies launch a big strike at the humans at the end and this wasn't an exception. The inevitable happened and the city is destroyed. I fail to see why this movie was given such good press when the acting and storyline are flawed in a big way. The film is just an excuse for the usual gore, blood and violence which for some sick, horrible reason Romero and all the people that enjoy watching his films love so much. Watch this if you like but it is truly very bad indeed.

The idea that the zombies will get more intelligent is an interesting continuation from Day of The Dead, the satire of America/the west is well done and interesting (like survival being dependent on a limited resource (food) in the hands of the zombies. Great stuff), but i cringed when the line "Call me Motown" was spoken. "Cool" code-names/nicknames in a zombie-movie? It was just jarring. The super vehicle Dead Reckoning was another bit that I really didn't like, along with most of the characters associated with it, especially "Pretty Boy" (Joanne Boland). In fact, the only character i found interesting from the "action movie posse" was Cholo (John Leguizamo). Most of the Dead Reckoning plot just stole time from the far more interesting part of the movie, the one with the intelligent zombies and the "safe" enclave of Fiddlers Green. The satire and social commentary in this part of the film is unfortunately drowned out by the action movie clichés surrounding "The hunt for Dead Reckoning". But it's not just that the action tries taking over the movie, it's also that most of the film is less interesting than what has gone before, or just bad. The action isn't as good as the action in the Dawn of the Dead remake, neither the "zombies gaining intelligence" plot or the "zombies ripping people to shreds" bit are as good as they are in Day of the Dead, the general lower quality of life in the post-apocalyptic world isn't really engaging and the satire was a little too obvious sometimes (Kaufman actually says "We don't negotiate with terrorists" in the movie).So, basically, land of the dead was a disappointment, trying to be too many things at once and thereby failing at all of them.

reviews.review_text: A well-paced, entertaining romp through the dark, zombiefied future as envisioned by acclaimed director George A. Romero.The lead character of Riley played by Simon Baker comes off as a bit too much of a good-natured boyscout. How he has managed to survive in this rough, gritty world is beyond me. Fortunately, his goody-goody nature is balanced by an excellent performance by John Leguizamo as the bad-ass soldier-for-hire Cholo. Dennis Hopper's villain, though one dimensional, is played seriously enough as to still evoke the viewer's disdain. Add a well-intentioned but misunderstood prostitute into the mix and a couple thousand zombies looming across the horizon and you've got an incredibly entertaining movie.

reviews.review_text: The good news: The last remaining survivors have gotten better organized. The bad news: So have the Zombies.I really wanted to like this movie, but alas, I just couldn't. I'm am a huge George A. Romero fan but this movie was disappointing. No plot to speak of and no real character development either. Which are two of the things that have always made Romero's horror movies stand out. It seems he has replaced these things in this movie with furious activity and action.In most of his earlier movies, there were small groups of people in simple settings, trying to survive. "Night of the Living Dead", a small group of people hiding out in a farmhouse. "Dawn of the Dead", survivors taking refuge in a shopping mall. "Day of the Dead", where a few military and scientists are in an underground shelter. In all these movies, the group of characters is small so there is a great deal of character development. Thus, you care about whether the people fighting the Zombies, live or die. Unfortunately, there's none of that in this movie, "Land of the Dead".Dennis Hopper, gives a wonderful performance, as usual, but it's just not nearly enough to carry this movie. John Leguizamo,as "Cholo", does not do much for the movie though. Is it just me or do others out there prefer that virtual unknowns be cast in Romero's movies? I don't like associating well known actors to other movies. I find it distracting, for some reason.At the end of the movie, Simon Baker's character "Riley" makes a sympathetic comment about the Zombies. Now, I don't know about you folks but I don't want to feel sorry for the Zombies, in my horror movies. It kind of ruins the dynamics, don't you think?? As Capt. Rhodes says in "Day of the Dead", "I don't want them to do anything but drop over!" This movie is horrible! I still love you though, George. :)

When I heard that Romero was making another "Of The Dead" film, I was excited. However after seeing the finished product, I have to say that I am disappointed. The story line is brilliant, very political and thought provoking, I did however find some of the characters to be lacking , and therefore felt no remorse when they died. The biggest disappointment, although it pains me to say, is the zombies. Well made up, but I would expect no less from the man who practically invented the modern image of a zombie, however their ability to learn, almost stupidly quickly, and with little explanation annoyed me. Why did the big black zombie possess much more intelligence than all of the others? In my mind, Bob (from day of the dead) should have taken the place of the black zombie. He was trained by the professor to have basic intelligence, and I think that would have made more sense. Another disappointment was the use of CGI. Obviously, this film was far more visually ambitious that his previous films, with huge explosions and such like, but I really did hope that Romero would show that the old school methods of special effects are still effective. There is a scene at the beginning of the film in which garbage is being dumped and a decomposing zombie is laying amongst the trash pile. For some reason, the effects when he is shot in the eye were done with CGI, which to be honest, sticks out like a sore thumb. There are several other moments which are ruined by the poor and rushed use of CGI which could have easily been achieved with a little more effort on physical props. All in all the film gets a positive review, because although I personally would have preferred the film to be made differently, it is still a very enjoyable, very gory, and could have been a lot worse. It looks like a Romero film from beginning to end, and will please old and new audiences alike.

reviews.review_text: I love the zombie genre and wanted to love this movie, and I was definitely biased in its favor. But aspects of it were unsatisfying.My biggest problem was the handling of Fidler's Green. I liked the idea of it but they should have explored the tension of trying to maintain normalcy in this last little bubble. Yes the rich people were living off the fruits of an exploitative system but it would have been much more interesting to have made them less shallow. This is one area where I think it was necessary to make things a little more realistic. I mean - aren't most of us living off the fruits of exploitative systems, blah, blah, blah? It's insulting that Romero thinks we'd miss the social commentary if he was less trite in his handling of the Fiddler's Green social system. In fact, any parallels to today's world would have been much more effective if he'd allowed the residents to be more human and identifiable.It's especially insulting in light of the fact that we're encouraged to empathize with the zombies. Like other posters, I was bugged when Simon Baker orders the zombies crossing the bridge to be spared because "like us - they're just looking for someplace to go". There are still going to be large numbers of people holed up in their apartments in the city. It's really not moving that the protagonist decides to just leave them to their fate because of some poetic identification with the zombies, especially when the zombies already have someplace to go - 99.999% of the earth.The one-dimensionality with which Fiddler's Green is handled is all the more striking in view of the inconsistencies that Romero allows his main character to have. Simon Baker's character should have been handled the way Mel Gibson's character was handled in Road Warrior: pessimistic and jaded but we're shown in subtle ways - rather than told - that he's not passed yearning for something different. Romero clumsily has his jaded, pessimistic hero come out and say nauseating things like "I'm looking for a world without fences." Right idea, wrong tactic.It's partly owing to the disaster movie-lover in me that I think there should have been more carnage scenes involving the destruction of the opulent world in Fiddler's Green. But I also think that it's unsatisfying that there was so much emphasis placed on this place and its demise is given so little screen time. And again, I think it would have better served Romero's social commentary if he'd focused on it. One deleted scene that was in the "Extra Bits" section of the DVD was a scene in which the corporate drone played by Peter Outerbridge (surprising to see in such a minor role)is shown trying to lead his family to safety after the zombies have invaded. Romero should have included scenes like this, if for no other reason, to reinforce how a corrupt system is as much a danger to those at the top, etc, etc.I also think it should have been more clear what was happening at the end. What was up with all the poor people walking along with their luggage? How had they survived? What was their celebratory air about? Yeah, their oppressors were dead but in light of everything we'd just watched, it seems the only thing that could be about to happen is the zombies will have regrouped and made a meal of them within ten minutes. And so "Big Daddy" and the other zombies being allowed to remain alive only adds to the confusion. The line from the Gilligan character indicates they're going to stay and try to build a better community. But they all look like they're heading somewhere, and we know that Simon Baker's character has decided to leave the city to the zombies. So just what are these people doing? The movie is annoying in what it decides to leave vague and what it goes way overboard in spelling out for us.

This movie delivers gore, social commentary, makes good use of modern special effects and has a good diverse cast.Like all Romero movies there is plenty of zombie feasting in this movie. Few are spared as limbs get torn of, people are chewed into, blood flows from a belly button and numerous zombies crowd over lone people eager for a good meal.The movie also carries on the tradition of Romeros social commentary of the time in which he is living. This time it is Cowboy Bush's America. The division of rich and poor, the iron fisted rule, crony capitalism, and bread and circuses to keep the poor quiet. Nice work George, very accurate if I do say so myself.The movie has the zombies as more sympathetic than the humans in a number of respects; Big Daddy cares for his subjects whereas Kaufman does not, the Zombies eat the humans merely because the disease makes them want to while a number of humans enjoy killing zombies and use them for entertainment and target practice. There are sympathetic humans however such as Riley, Slack and Charlie, and the poor residents of the city.This movie also adds a new dimension to the zombies, giving them a leader in Big Daddy (a zombie with emotion and greater intelligence than the other zombies), a hierarchy with Big Daddy's lieutenants, sees them reliving their pre-zombie lives, gives them learning abilities and new killing techniques (though these last two dimensions were touched on in Day of the Dead which I have not seen yet) including guns, knives, and petrol with fire.The movie also has a diverse cast playing a good characters, with Simon Baker as the pragmatic leader(an Aussie, yay) Asia Argento playing a confident and independent female lead, not merely a love interest, Robert Joy playing a mentally ill person with good marksmanship, John Leguazamo and Dennis Hopper also play their parts well. Also the movie is a representation of the New Hollywood with the acting abilities of other nations on display including Australla, Italy and Colombia. Modern day special effects are also put to use, but it doesn't ruin the fun or the gore. On top of all that the movie certainly isn't hard to follow, and can be just good plain fun as much as a social comment.Good cast, good social commentary, good fun, easy to watch, a nice effort from cast and crew. 9/10.

reviews.review_text: George A. Romero enters with yet another installment in his banal and grossly visual zombie flicks and hopefully this will be the last of them. Obviously there is an appreciative audience who enjoys watching partially decomposed bodies stomp around and grunt and eat body parts of the living because a lot of people write positively about this film.For this viewer the 'parody' eludes. LAND OF THE DEAD is simply a dark, grotesque, poorly written, hastily thrown together bit of treacle to make money off the folks who like this genre. But how fine actors like Simon Baker, John Leguizamo, Dennis Hopper, Asia Argento, and Robert Joy agree to the casting agent's invitation to star in this film is a conundrum. Grady Harp

reviews.review_text: · The Master returns with his fourth living dead entry, twenty years after his last dead release in 1985, Day of the Dead· This time around Romero bases his story around a population of approximately 3,500 people, entrenched within a fortified compound built around the downtown of an unnamed major US city· The city is protected by a private militarily based police force, owned and operated by the strong-hold's CEO, Kaufman, played effectively by Hopper whose character represents US corporate greed and selfishness· The city strong-hold is divided into two factions: The upper-class that had money before the zombie epidemic, who are able to live in a super security luxury compound; and the majority of the citizenry who were middle class before the outbreak, that are forced to live in ramshackle clusters based around the outskirts of the luxury compound· The middle and lower classes are sedated by pornography, gambling, drugs, and violence; and watched intensively by the police force· Kaufman has a professional scavenger force that goes outside the compound to gather essential and non-essential supplies from the zombie infested suburbs for consumption by both the rich and middle class· The main plot line of the film centers around one of Kaufman's scavenger manager's extortion of the city compound cash stockpile · More social commentary than living dead horror, Romero's fourth installment has drawn undue criticism from ignorant movie-goers· Admittedly, the film has more social messages than scary moments, but Romero attacks crucial social issues that are ignored by main-steam USA· Romero attacks the demise of the American middle class, minority struggles, corporate greed, and "the new" threat of terrorism · Unfortunately, many of the complaints lodged against this film are based around Romero's over-use of social allegories · I will admit however, that there could have been more scare and less preaching· The gore level is less than that of his previous dead films, which shows that Romero isn't making movies just to make people sick· There are several "jump scares" to satisfy the layman horror fan's appetite· This movie won't be truly appreciated until 2035 **********Ten out of ten stars **********Ten out of ten stars

reviews.review_text: I just saw Syriana and found its complexity in plot and character arresting. I have a feeling that the book on which it is based would flesh out some of my questions. I saw the book title and author in the closing credits, but forgot it as soon as I left the theater. I have a feeling that the book is perhaps too dense for a complete adaptation. This is not a criticism of a book that I have not yet read. I have never had the experience of finding the book on which a movie is based to be less interesting than the spin-off movie. I also find the lack of attention to the author and his work to be shameful. Why should the person who originated the thoughts that led to this movie adaptation be relegated to a place deep in the credits and nowhere on this website that I can find? However, I really appreciate that the movie operated at a level of implication rather than taking the usual American movie tack of being too explicit about motivation, character and plot. If anybody knows the title and author, could you please post it.

reviews.review_text: Has the movie industry lost its eye on the bottom line. I was dragged into this movie by a friend who paid for my ticket. I was in a couple of plays when I was in college, (one of my cast mates became a TV and Movie bit player). He used to tell me make up does not make up a good actor. This is a great, complex movie. Its only faults are in the clarity of character motivations. This is not a liberal or conservative film. It is an exploration into the existing system that evolved over many years.At no point in the movie does it take any pot-shots at Bush, Republicans, or Democracts. In fact, non of those words are ever spoken. It is not a left/right - red/blue debate. At no point in time does it ever mention the political parties of those in charge.The fact is, be it a Republican or Democrat, this world depends on oil. Our country while split on how to obtain it, will do anything to make sure the flow is not cut off.This movie finds faults with the global economy. Faults with the US system that has been tweaked by both sides over the span of decades. Faults with the Middle East for squandering its earnings. Faults with emerging China and its impact on consumption.Anyone claiming this movie is politically motivated is a troll looking for attention and should be ignored.

reviews.review_text: I liked Traffic (although I thought the original BBC mini-series was better.) I admire Gaghan's technique and his willingness to interweave different plot lines. I like the work of many of the actors here: Clooney, Cooper, Damon, Siddig, Wright, Peet, etc.That said, this movie is undone by the bias of the writer/director (and producers?) I don't doubt that there is corruption in the oil and natural gas industry. Gaghan doesn't want to tell the audience the truth, aside from the Saudis, the US just doesn't get much oil from the Persian Gulf. That oil and natural gas goes primarily to China and the rest of Asia, and secondarily to Europe. Yes, the US has supported non-democratic regimes (like the Saudis), but the real dirty-dealing has not been done by the US government and the CIA. It's been done by some Europeans and the Persian Gulf countries themselves. Witness the whole Iraq Oil-for-Food scandal, which the French petro-giant Total was involved with up to its eyeballs. Witness the revelation in the new Der Spielgel magazine in Germany that Iran has offered large amounts of oil to North Korea in exchange for help in developing nuclear weapons. Witness that Iran's Shahab 3 ICBM is essentially North Korean technology.That's the very real bad s**t that is taking place, NOT Gaghan's pipe dream. Hell, the South Park guys got closer to the truth in a puppet movie!

What a complete and utter waste of time this movie was! I saw it on opening night here in LA. Believe me, the people in the theater were a lot more excited BEFORE the film than they were AFTER it!! The plot is entirely too predictable and they have about 6 subplots that they HOPE are interesting enough for you to want to follow through to the end of the movie. believe me, after about the first 15 minutes of the film, you won't care about ANY of these subplots! They switch back and forth from each subplot so quickly that it gets confusing after a while. The acting, except for Chris Cooper, is second rate and not very believable. Clooney does a pretty good job, but is void of any real emotion or believability. I would ONLY recommend this movie if you are between the ages of 60 and 80 years old, and have absolutely NOTHING better to do with your time than watch some over-dramatic, dialog-loaded, boring waste of film for about 2 hours. I am a huge Clooney and Chris Cooper fan, but this is not their best work by a long shot. I wouldn't even recommend watching this movie on video, unless you are suffering from insomnia!

Complex and interesting, restored my faith in movies. Yes, it is difficult to follow, but the thinking person won't get lost. Don't bring Grandma or anyone with memory deficits. Never boring. Great performances all around. Would sustain repeat viewings. For anyone interested in the art of film editing, the work done here is particularly crisp and fine. Lensing by Robert Elswit is of Academy award caliber. Particularly daring is the portrait of the evolution of a suicide bomber. Plot takes twists and turns that cannot be anticipated. One of the side benefits of the film is the inescapable conclusion that the average American knows little about the Middle East or the forces at work that drove us to war, and there is much we will never know. On the down side, like many Hollywood films, this one presupposes our government and intelligence agencies to be far more clever and co-ordinated than they actually are, but that is the nature of most thrillers.

reviews.review_text: And based on the number of people who walked out of the theater I was not the only one who felt that way. I stuck around hoping to see it all tied together nicely but alas it was nothing special. The film was made along the same concept as Crash only without anything remotely interesting happening between the first scene and the last 10 minutes. Half way through the movie it is clear where the movie is going and how the story lines will eventually connect. Unfortunately, it takes way to long for things to happen. I was very intrigued by the concept presented in the trailers and based on the reviews on IMDb was excited to see Syriana. This is definitely a "wait till it comes out on video" selection.

I just saw this film in LA. I, personally, found it to be rather long and confusing- so many different subplots going on. However, if you have the patience to weather it out, it can have a payoff (I guess). Fortunately, I brought along someone intelligent who explained the finer points of the plot to me afterwords! It turns out one of the main points of the movie is how these countries with oil could be better organized & work together- resulting in the ability to invest what they get & build a stabler society. This, however, isn't in the interest of the oil companies-- they want chaos so they can maintain the control. My advice: drink lots of caffeine before seeing the film & bring along someone else in case you get lost.

When a complex plot with enigmatic characters serve to draw the audience in and keep it fully engaged, a political thriller is successful.Unfortunately, Syriana appears to have been made by a filmmaker who had forgotten he was making this film for an audience; that the people in the seats were flesh and blood, breathing humans who had paid for a ticket expecting a story and characters who were also made out of flesh and blood.Instead we get stick figures who have been drawn with only slight changes in facial expressions whom Gaghan woodenly moves around the globe, uttering completely wooden, bloodless (yet overblown) dialogue.If his point was to show there is no soul involved in any aspect of the oil industry, I "get it." But did he have to numb my emotions, insult my intelligence and completely bore me to death for over two hours to illustrate his point? Is this my punishment for being a consumer of oil?

To have such an ambitious, wide-ranging plot coldly and rather confusingly executed represents a terrific opportunity wasted. If only the writer/director melded the ingredients with greater clarity and emotional weight. The corruption, double-dealing and greed of governments and individuals, more pertinent now than ever, should have lent itself to a powerful, devastating film. Yes, we leave the theater with our increasingly cynical views of the world confirmed. But the film should have done more for an audience already jaded before the lights went down. This is no MISSING, the absorbing Costa-Gravas film which almost from its beginning, left the audience enthralled and unusually uneasy. That political film both provoked and entertained.

I thought Syriana did its job. I enjoyed the film, and as a person who's spent time in the Middle East, found its portrayal of some of the sub cultures in the region quite accurate. However my posting is more to clarify some things about the movie and where the characters are supposed to come from...The main one being about the young 'Palestinian man'. He actually isn't Palestinian. Most expatriate workers in the Gulf come from South Asian countries, such as India and Pakistan. The 'Palestinian man' was in fact from Pakistan, as were his friends.They were speaking Urdu. The man who gave him the missile is the only Arab in that story (about the Islamic school). Yes they spoke Arabic at times (when he was speaking to his teacher), but to his father and his friends, he was not speaking Arabic. Just out of curiosity, how many viewers do you think actually followed that there were at least 4 languages spoken in the movie (excluding French)? Arabic, Farsi, English, Urdu (and maybe some Punjabi?). I think it's important to know these little details because it helps the audience really understand who is being affected (not just young, frustrated Arab men).

Here's a quick thumbnail sketch of the many plots of the new Focus Features release, "Syriana," starring George Clooney, Matt Damon, Christopher Plumber and Chris Cooper: Story 1) Bob Barnes (Clooney) is a CIA covert operative in the Middle East. An expert in this region, he speaks Farsi, is tight with Hezbollah and even infiltrated al-Qeada.Story 2) Energy expert and financial consultant, Bryan Woodman (Damon) lives a great life in Geneva with his lovely wife, Julie (Amanda Peet, "The Whole 10 Yards") and his two adorable little boys.Story 3) Attorney Bennett Holiday (Jeffrey Wright, "Broken Flowers") is hired by a Connex Oil Co. bigwig (Christopher Plummer, "The Insider") to find out any dirt on Connex's proposed merger with the small Kemmer Corporation before the Feds do. It seems that Kemmer has procured a deal with the vast oil fields of Kasakistan while Connex has just lost a big Saudi contract to the Chinese.Story 4) A young Arab (Olivier Yglesias), despondent and unemployed because of the merger, is recruited into a radical Muslim terrorist organization.And Story 5) A Saudi king passes up his oldest son, Prince Nasir (Alexander Siddig) - a reformer and visionary who desires to bring progress and civil rights to his country - in favor of his less-qualified younger brother (Sam Georges said) who, conveniently, supports keeping US troops in his country.That's basically the plot setup. Now the wheels begin to turn. Barnes is assigned by the CIA to arrange the assassination of Nasir; instead he is subjected to brutal torture by a rogue terrorists, led by Mussawi (Mark Strong, "Oliver Twist"). Woodman becomes Nasir's chief financial adviser after his son's tragic death. Holiday, working with Kemmer honcho Jimmy Pope, finds a crooked connection in that company's big deal, and offers to cut a deal with the US Attorney's office. Later, after some bungling, the agency distances itself from Barnes, who heads to Saudi Arabi in an attempt to stop another plot against Nasir. Competently written and directed by Stephan Gaghan (who won a screenplay Oscar in 2000 for "Traffic," another complex, multi-layered film, this time about the drug trade), "Syriana" can be seen as either a cerebral, thoughtful, intelligent, complex motion picture, or a convoluted, confusing mishmash of a movie.To me, it's a little bit of both, with the overriding message that oil ruins everything it touches and the United States, with its secret dealings, underhanded alliances and shady involvement in other governments, is pretty much evil. Many people, however, may run out of patience before the movie ends (which seems to be almost glacial at times).Evidently, Gaghan did a lot of research here, especially with Saudi royalty, and the intricate plots show this; likewise, the many location shots give a true, gritty feel to the picture. Use of Arabic and Farsi (along with English subtitles) also gives the movie a realistic look.The acting, on the other hand, leaves something to be desired. Damon is his usual cute boy self; Peet is non-descript; Plummer is menacingly devious; and Clooney (bloated and bearded for the role) seems to sleepwalk through the role. It is a huge contrast to his dynamic work in the terrific "Good Night And Good Luck." I cannot say I enjoyed the film; but it was a decent effort which deserves a look. Whether that mild recommendation means anything, I can't say. I have a feeling, though, that it will not translate into very big box office.

reviews.review_text: Looking for an escapist movie free of political propaganda? See something else. Looking for a complicated thriller where seemingly disconnected plot lines neatly converge after two hours with brilliant acting by all, this is for you.This may decomplicate the plot weave a smidge: George Clooney plays a veteran CIA operative on the down-stroke of his career selling explosives and arms to Iran terrorists; Energy analyst (Matt Damon) is recruited to advise Crown Prince Nasir (Alexander Siddig). Nasir, the wiser of two brothers vying to succeed the retiring Emir for his kingdom. Nasir wants to evict the wicked American Oil company so Communist Chinese oil enterprise can step in (  yipes!) for the ultimate good of his country. There's this American Oil company (Connex) which is considering a merger with a much smaller oil company (Killen) that holds the exclusive Kazakhstan oil drilling rights.  Connex's lawyers send an attorney (Jeffrey Wright) to discover just how Killen "got" those rights before the SEC does. (The SEC, you see, has to approve the merger) And then we have your Pakistani migrant oil workers suddenly confronting the realities of unemployment after the Chinese take over. They're recruited by a religious fanatic after yet another spell of idle poverty.The film provides perspective on why and how things can get "confused" in this part of the world. Weirder still: that the Chinese and the religious zealots come off as the good guys as the evil US oil companies make prey out of Nasir, justifying corruption for their version of a greater good. It's a well made film. But, man-o-man, for simpler entertainment, check out that Harry Potter and his Fire Goblet. For this one, wear your thinking cap and bring your paranoia defenses. 7 out of 10 . . . for the acting.

reviews.review_text: I recently saw this movie and was expecting it to be a lot better; however I was very disappointed in the way it turned out. I am from Dubai, the United Arab Emirates and did not like the fact that it was named as "the Persian Gulf" also, most of the film was shot in the worst areas of the Arab world and the movie viewed the whole middle east as if it were ONE country. When they showed the best part of Dubai which is one of the hotels they named it as "SPAIN"!!! That really annoyed me because its NOT Spain, i mean how could Arabs be ruling Spain? that was dumb. The idea portrayed behind all that politics made sense and in some ways were very true but it does not apply to every single country in the middle east and neither to every single American. The movie was disorganized in my opinion and could have been much better because the idea was very clever.

I was fortunate enough to see a screening of this where the director did a Q&A afterwords. He explained how he had spent months traveling and writing and researching in the Middle East (including the Gulf). He insisted on shooting the film in rarely shown nations like Dubai. I could feel this reality seeping through the film. The actors too were cast from people from Morrocco to India. The director wanted real people who spoke real dialects in the roles. This detail worked for me. I have been to the Middle East and to North Africa a number of times and this film felt right. The people that I met on my travels treated me with a bizarre and mysterious mix of truth and lies, of hospitality and resentment, of graciousness and blame. The film captured this. The performances were well delivered, the story was intricate and clear enough and the end left good questions open. My favorite scene was with Christopher Plumber on the boat when he shows what real power is to the paper tiger prince. I think this is a must see. As an American it must be seen.

reviews.review_text: I'm intrigued by the film's subject matter. I felt it was a bit too ambitious with the weaving in and out of the complex characters. It could have just stuck with the big picture, (i.e. why are we so dependent on foreign oil?) Excellent acting. Great insight into dirty CIA tactics and Texas oil strategies. The Hezzbollah angle was confusing for me. I'm not afraid to admit that it was a bit too complex for me upon my initial viewing, I'll probably need to rent the DVD. It also did a good job of showing how easy it is to convert indifferent young men in the middle east to extreme Islam. It maximizes it's 2 hour length for all it's worth. Don't go to the restroom or you'll have some catching up to do.

I thoroughly enjoyed Syriana, however, it probably is not for all types of movie views. Let me say first of all, I am a bleeding heart liberal, and that was one of my main motivations for going to see the movie. People of opposite political persuasions might not enjoy the movie as much, I think, because the way you take the end of the movie might depend on how you feel about government, not particularly the current American government or even the American government in general. If you are disenchanted with international politics, this movie will probably strike your fancy.Also, it is very hard to keep track of what is going on, mostly because the movie is not directed like most other movies, with a flowing plot. The best example I can think of is Lord of the Rings, because it is a bunch of simultaneous plot lines running together that culminate at the end. However, whereas LoTR only had two real plot lines, Syriana has at least 3, maybe more.Concluding, it is a very well conceived movie, well directed, and very interesting. However, if you are looking for an edge-of-your-seat-Jerry-Bruckheimer type explosion adventure, you will not find it in Syriana. Don't let the explosion in the previews fool you.

reviews.review_text: I liked this and respect the heck outta what they were trying to do, but there are times while watching it that you can be forgiven for forgetting who is who, why they are doing what they are doing, and so on and so forth.Take Christopher Plummer. Now I kept on forgetting-was he a lawyer? An Enron-style oil guy? He was also mentioned by Clooney as having been 'in Beirut before', which makes you wonder if he was a former CIA type himself back in the day. That took some getting used to.Then there's Clooney. Now I kept thinking that he was in Beirut to go after whomever it was that swiped his Rocket in the opening scenes. I didn't quite figger that he was out to kill Emir Son 1, which goes to show you how much attention I was paying perhaps.Then there's all the oil guys. You can't remember a name with a face. Sure Chris Cooper played a JR Ewing type, but what was his name? When they start rattling off 6-7 oil bigwigs' names off, Jeffrey Wright does I mean up in that office tower, you can believe I was lost along with the rest of the audience.I had to re-read some of these reviews here to get these things aligned right in my mind.What worked? Matt Damon and his family. Good stuff there. Peet had a small role but she was fine. I liked the 'good Prince's' role. Clooney was good if lower-keyed here. Plummer, William Hurt(!-cameo!), Cooper-all fine. Enjoyed the locales.The Human Bombers/Al-Qaeda recruits who go to their demise on that boat which strikes the tanker at the end--a good storyline too. All too believable.I think a more linear plot line might not have hurt? but it's worthy of your attention just the same.*** outta ****.

reviews.review_text: I was very impressed by this film. It's a slick production with excellent cinematography, and at the same time intelligent and well acted. Those four elements don't often come together. Nobody, from the suicide bomber and radical clerics to the CIA hit man to the corrupt oil executives to the Arab princes are portrayed as simplistically good or bad, but rather as people in different places and situations, which is what they are. That's rare for a mainstream movie, and refreshing.The movie definitely has strong echoes of Traffic, but is both more serious: the characters are less cartoonish, and while the cocaine trade is something in which most of us have only a voyeuristic interest, Syriana's subject matter affects us all, and the attitude that this film takes is a reflection of that.By the way, to the people upset because this movie portrays the oil industry and Washington insiders as 'bad', A) you are missing the point, and B) you are living in a dream world. Wake up!

reviews.review_text: When we were choosing a movie to see on New Year's Day, I said (smugly) to my wife that if we were to see "Syriana" at the suburban multiplex 14, we would have the theater to ourselves. Much to my surprise, the 7 PM showing was nearly sold-out, and we had to find our seats along with other adults desperate for an intelligent offering. The movie was never less than fascinating, and admirable for its exploration of serious (but not necessarily ticket-selling) themes. There was a book written in the 1950s titled "The Nature of the Non-Western World", and I couldn't get the title out of my mind when I watched this film. How rare is it that we see characters living their lives not as stereotypical America- haters but as complex, yearning people who are both fascinated and troubled by Western culture.This is a remarkable, difficult, rewarding film. I thought that the golden age of smart, socially-involved movies were gone. There appears to be some hope.

reviews.review_text: I wasn't going to write a review of this and it will become clear later why not. I had tried to get to see it a number of times and interestingly enough, could not get any 'local' feedback, meaning that none of my friends had seen it and none were too enthusiastic, for some unidentifiable reason, about attending a screening.So with the nomination of George Clooney for the supporting actor Oscar, I felt compelled to go. I attended an extremely comfortable suburban theater with huge seats and a big screen on the afternoon of Oscar night. I am getting somewhere with all of this, please trust me.George is good in this, in a lot of the bits I saw and a lot of the bits the other nineteen people in the theatre saw. We all agreed on this as we left the theatre. He wasn't Oscar worthy, we thought, but a good performance, and he looked interestingly decayed and used up with the extra weight and the bags under the eyes.You see, I fell asleep on and off throughout the film as did the other nineteen people who were in attendance with me. We sheepishly looked around at each other throughout the screening as we all took turns to catch a few zzzzs. The script, well, it never grabbed, and while understanding that the film was not linear, well it got really, really confusing, you couldn't quite unpick all the threads, we knew the child died but did he appear again as a ghost? And why? What was that ending? What was George doing in it? Where was his wife? Was she CIA too? I hate movies where you have to work this hard, it gets so exhausting you have to catnap now and again. We took it upon ourselves, we the audience, to rotate our sleep shifts.I can't rate it. Not fair. But if you're a chronic insomniac, this movie could really, really help you. George was not Oscar-winner worthy, that shoulda gone to Jake.

Obviously it depends on your politics but those who share mine say that we are in Iraq because of the West's demand for oil. They say that top US politicians are in bed with the Saudi Royal family because of oil. They say that corruption is rife within the corridors of power in regards oil dealing and even that those who demand oil for their sports utility vehicles are guilty of funding terrorists by not controlling their consumption. Now, given that this is a subject that we all believe to be swimming in corruption and shady going-ons, you do have to wonder why Gaghan was not able to pull it together into a tighter, more meaningful and more impacting narrative.Many of the professional reviews I have read for this film have complained that the stories are hard to connect and that it gave you the feeling you'd walked in late and missed something; however the same reviews also forgive this by saying "maybe that was the point". Well, maybe it was but that is not an excuse for having a film that is about two hours long that only starts to come together towards the end. It does not forgive the subplots that don't add value or the scenes that don't fit simply because the script doesn't tell us until the end how it is going to work. Of course the film still engaged me because the individual threads were all interesting even if their relevance or direction was not always clear, but it was a problem for me that they were so disconnected  and that may well be the point but it doesn't make for a great film. Equally disappointing was how simplistic the connection ultimately was and how obvious the point made were; again, maybe it is because we all assume these things to be true that this was not an eye-opener and shocking condemnation that it should have been.Many viewers will struggle to get into a film that seems intent on pushing the viewer away. We are given things that seem to go nowhere, stories that don't seem to connect, characters we are not allowed to understand and we are left wondering when it will get to the place we know it is all going. It is still worth a look though because individual scenes are great and even the individual threads have enough to make them interesting but it is just such a shame that all these little things don't come together very well. As director Gaghan has done a great job because the film looks great, moves nicely and looks really professional. Likewise the cast are impressive in their presence as well as performances (on the whole) if you ignore the limitations the materials serves them with. Clooney is impressive and it is not his fault that his character doesn't totally make sense. Plummer relishes his powerful old man but Wright doesn't seem to know what to do with his and he seems to either have it all going on inside his head or he just didn't understand what he was doing. Damon is good but again I don't think he saw how he was meant to fit in. Support from Peet, Waked, Cooper, Foxworth, Novak and others is all fine but they cannot overcome the problems inherent in the story and the telling.Overall then this is worth seeing but fell way short of my expectations. It looks great and the cast are all good on paper and on screen but the narrative problems just completely undercut it for me. I know that Gaghan was going for a tapestry of stories to all come together but he didn't pull it off and instead of being one impressive tapestry it is a patchwork quilt  bits of it are good but stand back from it and it all works disjointed and messy. Interesting but nowhere near good enough to be compared to Traffic, which does the same thing but actually pulls it off.

As a thriller 'Syriana' isn't particularly thrilling. It has much of worth to say about the responsibility of the West for the continuing crisis in the Middle East, and about the duplicities of the oil industry, internationally, but the overall tone of Steven Gaghan's script is so polemical and the outcome (in broad terms) predictable that it loses momentum.That's not to say it isn't an entertaining film. It is. There are splendid performances from principals Clooney, Damon, the underrated Jeffrey Wright and Siddig, and superb supporting turns from the likes of Chris Cooper, Tim Blake Nelson, Amanda Peet, William Hurt and (at his most reptilian) Christopher Plummer. The film has much of worth to say about the consequences of American foreign policy with regard to the oil trade and the wilful manipulations of Arab states. There are some electric sequences, too, but  the occasional explosion aside  very few surprises. It's too damned expository.Part of the problem concerns the three leading men  the CIA operative (Clooney), the economic adviser (Damon) and the lawyer investigating possible corruption within the US oil trade (Wright). The first is a patriot who manipulates or murders on the orders of his government, and who is surprised when he is in turn manipulated. The interests of the second are entirely governed by profit. The third seeks corruption, but profits, professionally, from selling out one of his bosses to another. This may, perhaps, be an attempt to signal to audiences that these are not reactionary anti-American caricatures  the characters all have a vested interest in the status quo  but they are not particularly likable. Neither are they virtuous or heroic  though a last-gasp attempt is made to turn Clooney's conflicted agent into such a character  though even his change of perspective is principally prompted by being made a whipping-boy by his agency rather than altruism. Unfortunately this effort is too little too late, and the character's motivations are rather muddled by the labyrinthine plotting.It's an interesting film, but if I didn't share the liberal politics of the film-makers I don't think I would necessarily have thought so.

This movie is very unorthodox for a Hollywood-movie, both in the story itself, how the story is presented, and the fact that there is a noticeable absence of slick Hollywood characters or glamour.It's a complex action drama, and although it moves slower than the average action drama nowadays, it moves deeper and with 10 times the information and it took me some time to get overview of the film. The acting is of highest quality on all accounts.This movie is a must-see, but comes with a warning: Don't see the movie unless you are up for it. With 4 story lines intertwining, you need to be clear headed and awake.

reviews.review_text: I didn't agree with all of the premises of Syriana; nevertheless I thought it was a fine, engaging piece of film making, which showed the courage to ask hard questions that most supposedly 'topical' films don't. If I have one gripe, it's that the movie needed to work dramatically as well as polemically; for the most part it did, yet the ending undermined it. The film makers wanted a big climax but forget to make it consistent with the rest of the intricate story. The reason that Clooney's character is framed as a rogue operative is that his CIA cohorts don't want it to be suspected that they were behind Clooney's failed plot to assassinate an Arab leader. However, they then decide to assassinate the same Arab leader (Alexander Siddig) in a completely blatant and traceable way by targeting him with a satellite guided missile. Yes it sets up a taut ending: Clooney realizing Siddig is not the terrorist he'd been led to believe tries to avert the killing; but it makes no sense and for an otherwise intelligent thriller this was a let down.

reviews.review_text: "Syriana" is a movie that should be watched several times to truly absorb it's plot and it's point. Most of the actors do an excellent job with Amanda Peet being the lone exception. She doesn't have the depth to really make her small role memorable. However, everyone else really shines.It's a movie that packs a powerful punch. It doesn't quite finish the job, though. I've heard that there is at least one sub-blot and lots of other scenes that have hit the cutting room floor. Rumored to be because of a preview audience's reaction to, at the time, the long running time of the film. The movie clocks in at just about two hours. This is one of the few times I've thought a film could have used another half hour.Still, you should see it because there's nothing like it out there. It is one of the few films to show the Middle East as it is, without everyone wearing White or Black hats. You can debate the film's politics if you like, but there's no denying that oil is one of the main reasons for the chaos in that region.

reviews.review_text: (There's a big spoiler towards the end, marked SPOILER!).Syriana deals with it's subject matter very well. It's so refreshing to see a film that portrays the complexity of US/global politics in a relatively balanced way instead of dumbing down it for the box-office or political means. However, this is where it fails, as well.The plot is too complex and interesting to be dealt with in the running-time of the film. The pace was too jumpy and the character development was to insufficient to allow me to really get involved. About a a third of the way into the film I decided that I had missed too much to continue so restarted the DVD with the resolve to concentrate more. This certainly helped but I still had to rewind a few parts where I'd missed important dialogue or wasn't sure who somebody was.I believe it would have been fantastic as, say a TV/DVD mini series. This would have allowed more time to develop the characters, who all had an interesting story to tell and allow things to build, almost in real-time. And, imagine the political discussions, rants and outrages that each episode would provoke (I guess I'm remembering Twin Peaks - I haven't seen Lost!).SPOILER: The final attack on Prince Nasir was a big let down compared to the rest of the film. It was so cheesy and unrealistic. Was it rewritten for the studio or something - it seemed that way? I just could not believe the stupidity of stopping the convey on the way to the coup because of a flock of sheep, however enlightened and liberal the Prince had become. They could have driven round, as demonstrated by Bob a couple of minutes later! And what the hell was Bob doing? Why didn't he just text or email a warning? Why didn't the guards shoot him? I could just about suspend belief for the unlikely way that they were assassinating the Prince, but this was just silly and unnecessary. Why even bother to kill Bob - let him suffer in his impotence to undo the chain of events that he has helped initiate, and find out what happened to his 2nd missile. Also why save through Bryan Woodman luck? END OF SPOLERTo conclude, it's a nice change to see a film that deals with US/global political issues intelligently, without taking extreme or dumb viewpoints (e.g. Michael Moore) but too short-running to tell a good story, and a bit silly towards the end. Definitely worth having on DVD so you can watch it several times.

reviews.review_text: I look forward to watching this film again as there was just so much happening it really is difficult to absorb it all in one viewing. Having said that, this is one of the best movies I've seen of late. It's only let down by the fact that it feels like they had to cut a lot out of the film to make it only two hours long. It jerks along in parts, at times too quickly and I often felt like going back over a scene with the remote control to see what I must have missed. It asks a lot of the viewer, but overall it is brilliant. This is the way to make a film with a message. It doesn't hit it's audience with a sledgehammer and although there is some quite disturbing violence, it is very realistic and makes many valid and disturbing points.There is a array of great actors in this film and George Clooney does stand out, but overall the cast were outstanding. I found some of the reality in the film was unconvincing. For example, underwater pool lighting is always low voltage, not mains voltage.Unfortunately, I'm convinced that this is probably how it really is amongst business and government and it shows us all how little influence we have on our own lives, although the ending offers us all a glimmer of hope.

reviews.review_text:
A superb film, and a magnificent introduction to the problems in the Middle East. It does not take sides, it cuts open the political cant with a scalpel, not a hatchet, the film has more finesse than a rant from Oliver Stone, and reveals that there are two sides to every conflict. In this respect the film is a breath of fresh air. Consistent and at times unwatchable, it gives you that queasy feeling that you just may not be on the side of the 'good guys'. Frankly a brave movie to make, especially in the current political climate that exists in the US, every bit as subversive as Citizen Kane.

Don't trust the normally reliable ratings here, its actually an 8.8 movie, too many voters here just can't digest the message, and probably voted against it. I confess, I had some difficulty coming to terms with the 'point of view'. A courageous movie, well acted, well scripted, and well made.

reviews.review_text:
It's been less than a week since I watched this film and I don't remember much about it. It just was not very entertaining and it was hard to pay attention since it is way too long. Too many characters and too little time devoted to each one. I still have no idea what the point of Matt Daman's character was.

And I have no idea why George Cloony won acting awards for this role. I didn't think it was anything exceptional. He plays a CIA(I think) agent who plays undercover roles in the Mid East. His story involves a king and a brother and something about him trying to stop an assassination. Plus, he gets tortured by some guy who the first time we see them together seems like his friend. I didn't get that.

The whole subject matter was just boring.

FINAL VERDICT: Did not deserve the praise it received last year. Boring. A waste of time.

"Syriana" tells many different stories that overlap. George Clooney is something like a CIA officer who goes to foreign countries and makes things go smoother for America by eliminating problems and people. Matt Damon is a broker for an oil company, who negotiates with Middle Easterners. We have the story of two brothers (one who was Dr. Bashir on "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine") who might grow up to be king -- one pro-American and the other not so much. And we have Arab youths who discover a rocket and are unsure what to do with it.

This movie is well-acted, well-scripted and well-directed. The plot is deep and thick, and the actors all do their part to make it as wonderful as possible. Even supporting actors (like Amanda Peet) are amazing. This is also the movie's downside, because it is next to impossible you will fully understand what you're seeing on the first viewing: so much depth and interwoven plot lines. (But, again, if a film make you want to watch it again, perhaps this is good?) George Clooney's character (Bob Barnes) is relatively minor in the first half, but he plays a much bigger role later on. You see how torture and terrorism works up close (from both American and Arab points of view) and what the government will do to you if they feel threatened. Very gripping, very emotional -- and one scene which is disgusting (but crucial to drive the point home).

You might wonder, "can I sit through such a long movie?" Well, can you? I guess the movie was originally even longer, and I wish they would release a director's cut (maybe they have). The average viewer won't want anything beyond two hours, but I'd take three... just to get more story from this well of goodness.

If you like great directing, acting, writing... rent this movie. If you care about the Middle East or America's role in it, rent this. If you care about the politics of oil, rent this. I think it is safe to say this film has something of a liberal bias, but there is nothing shown that (to my knowledge) isn't completely factual -- and sometimes we need the truth blunt in our face like this, like a boot to the crotch.

reviews.review_text: There's more to the movie than the Clooney Oscar! Much more. So much more that you have to keep your eyes open, all the time! Because if you blink or if you don't listen carefully enough you might miss something. And if that happens, you might not understand the whole movie! Which would be tragic, because this movie has a lot to say! It's overly political of course, but not in the sense of taking the side of democrats/republicans, but by letting you see what is going on behind the scenes. The movie is shot/edited in a way that, has also worked in the movie "Traffic" (Soderbergh), also with multiple story lines.The movie shows a complex political situation that might leave you baffled & speechless. That were my feelings after I watched the movie and also a pain & anger at what is going on in the world ... a tragedy!!

reviews.review_text: The oil empire, fusion of companies, CIA, the US Justice department, the corrupt monarchies of Middle and Near East, the conflict between the people's interests and the interests of big oil corporations, a prince that tries to put an end to the alliance between his country and a foreign power which has military bases on its soil, Hezbollah and the suicide attackers all these ingredients are admirably mixed and intertwined in this movie with much truth and realism. The syncopated cut makes its visual message very efficient by means of short sequences contrasting quickly very different atmospheres and sceneries, jumping for instance from a desert scene showing the poor immigrant oil workers to a scene of a meeting of the oil tycoons in a posh office in America or Europe or even Beirut. A very important movie for the portrait of a true reality it displays and for the implicit message it conveys.

reviews.review_text: I have been reading some of the reviews here. Those who are critical of it seem to think that the movie portrays USA too negatively and it is the ARABS who are to be blamed for the current oil crisis. I think this movie actually shows how America, at the behest of American companies seem to think that they can do anything to anyone just because they have the military power. This movie shows how corrupt Americans are destroying the Middle East. The movie in itself is very good. The characters are well built. The character of the young suicide bomber has been portrayed very responsibly. This is a certainly a movie which forces you to think. If people find it difficult to follow the story then it is their fault.
